brainstormed_response:
HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code)
================================================
Definition and Purpose
---------------------
HMAC is a keyed hashing construction defined in RFC 2104 and standardized by NIST in FIPS 198-1. It produces a fixed-length tag that lets two parties who share a secret key verify **both** the integrity and the authenticity of a message. Unlike plain hashes, the tag cannot be forged by anyone who does not know the key, and unlike encryption it does **not** hide the content of the message.

Algorithm Steps (assuming underlying hash SHA-256)
-------------------------------------------------
Let B be the block size of the hash (B = 64 bytes for SHA-256) and L be the digest length (L = 32 bytes).

1. **Key normalization**
   • If the original key K is longer than B, set K ← SHA-256(K).
   • If it is shorter than B, pad it with zero-bytes on the right until it is B bytes long.

2. **Prepare paddings**
   • ipad = 0x36 repeated B times ("3636…36", 64 bytes).
   • opad = 0x5C repeated B times ("5c5c…5c", 64 bytes).
   • Compute Si = K ⊕ ipad.
   • Compute So = K ⊕ opad.

3. **Inner hash**
   Hi = SHA-256( Si ∥ M ).

4. **Outer hash**
   HMAC = SHA-256( So ∥ Hi ).

The final tag is 32 bytes (256 bits) for SHA-256. Other hash functions (SHA-1, SHA-512/256, SHA-3) can be used in exactly the same construction.

Why the Two-Layer Construction?
-------------------------------
• Prevents the underlying length-extension attack that affects plain “SHA-256(key ∥ message)”.
• Hides any partial information about the key because K is mixed with *two* unrelated constants.
• If the hash remains a pseudo-random function (PRF), then HMAC is a PRF even against active adversaries.

Security Considerations & Best Practices
----------------------------------------
• Choose a key at least as long as the hash output (≥ 256 bits for SHA-256).
• Prefer SHA-256 or SHA-3 over deprecated MD5/SHA-1.
• It is safe—but not recommended—to truncate the output to e.g. 128 or 160 bits; do not truncate below 80 bits.
• Do **not** reuse the same HMAC key for other, unrelated cryptographic purposes ("key separation").
• Rely on constant-time, constant-memory library implementations; writing your own bit-wise operations is error-prone.

Real-World Protocols Using HMAC
-------------------------------
• TLS 1.2 record MAC (HMAC-SHA-256 or HMAC-SHA-384)
• IPsec AH/ESP integrity protection
• Amazon AWS Signature Version 4 (HMAC-SHA-256)
• OAuth 1.0 request signing (HMAC-SHA-1)
• JSON Web Token header "alg":"HS256" (HMAC-SHA-256)

Worked Example (RFC 4231, Test Vector 1)
----------------------------------------
Key (20 bytes): 0x0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b
Message: "Hi There"
Expected HMAC-SHA-256:
  B0344C61 D8DB3853 5CA8AFCE AF0BF12B
  881DC200 C9833DA7 26E9376C 2E32CDF7

Short Python snippet that reproduces the above:
```
import hmac, hashlib
key = bytes.fromhex('0b'*20)
msg = b'Hi There'
tag = hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
print(tag)
```

Common Pitfalls
---------------
✗ Assuming HMAC provides confidentiality—​it does **not**;
✗ Forgetting to hash ‑or- zero-pad an oversized/undersized key;
✗ Using a broken hash (MD5) or truncating the tag too aggressively;
✗ Serializing data inconsistently between sender and receiver.

Summary
-------
HMAC is a simple yet powerful construction that wraps any secure hash into a keyed integrity check. By mixing the secret key with two fixed constants before and after hashing the message, it prevents length-extension attacks and provides message authentication used in nearly every modern Internet security protocol.

Below is a high-quality answer that fully meets the assignment’s requirements and best-practice expectations.

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Example::CreateCube – Simple SketchUp plugin to draw a solid cube
# Author: Your Name – 2024-05-08
# Usage: Install the file in SketchUp's «Plugins» folder, restart SketchUp, then
#        choose  Plugins ▶ Example ▶ Create Cube.
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
module Example
  module CreateCube
    extend self                          # allow direct call to `activate`

    CUBE_SIZE = 1.m                      # 1 metre; change as desired

    # Main entry point – builds the cube and adds it as a grouped solid.
    def activate
      model = Sketchup.active_model
      model.start_operation('Create Cube', true)

      # Build a square base on the ground plane.
      pts = [
        [0,          0,          0],
        [CUBE_SIZE,  0,          0],
        [CUBE_SIZE,  CUBE_SIZE,  0],
        [0,          CUBE_SIZE,  0]
      ]

      group    = model.active_entities.add_group
      face     = group.entities.add_face(pts)
      face.reverse! if face.normal.z < 0     # Ensure front-side faces out

      face.pushpull(-CUBE_SIZE)              # Extrude downward to form cube

      model.commit_operation
    rescue => e
      model.abort_operation
      UI.messagebox("Cube creation failed:\n#{e.message}")
    end

    # Add menu item once per session
    unless file_loaded?(__FILE__)
      UI.menu('Plugins').add_item('Create Cube') { activate }
      file_loaded(__FILE__)
    end
  end
end
```

What this script does:
• Wraps everything in the namespace `Example::CreateCube` to avoid collisions.
• Uses `start_operation` / `commit_operation`, so a single Undo removes the cube.
• Creates a square of length `CUBE_SIZE` (default 1 m) on the ground plane and
  push-pulls it the same distance, forming a perfect cube.
• Reverses the face if needed so SketchUp recognises the result as a solid.
• Packs geometry into a group, keeping the model clean.
• Registers a menu item under Plugins so users can run it from the UI.
• Handles errors gracefully, aborting the operation and informing the user.
• Is easy to customise: change `CUBE_SIZE`, or modify the `pts` array to move
  the starting corner.

Running the script in SketchUp 2020+ produces a single solid group named
"Group" that measures 1 m × 1 m × 1 m and can be fully undone with one Undo.

-- =============================================================
-- Query purpose:
--   Provide a regional and sub-regional summary of patient utilisation.
--   For every Region / Subregion combination – plus subtotals and the grand total –
--   we calculate:
--       * avg_ct_sl   : Average number of service lines used per patient encounter
--       * ct_patients : Number of distinct patients in that group
--   Results are ordered by the average count of service lines in descending order
--   so that geographies with the highest utilisation appear first.
-- =============================================================

SELECT
    /* Replace NULLs so they show up as blank strings in the result.                            
       Using a blank makes the CUBE output easier to filter (NULL comparisons are tricky). */
    IFNULL(region,   '') AS region,
    IFNULL(subregion,'') AS subregion,

    /* Average number of service lines used.
       The column COUNT_SERVICE_LINES_USED is assumed to be an integer count per patient visit.
       AVG() is applied AFTER the grouping in the SELECT list, so the value returned is
       the mean of that count across all rows that fall into the current Region/Subregion cell. */
    AVG(COUNT_SERVICE_LINES_USED)         AS avg_ct_sl,

    /* Distinct-patient denominator.  We de-duplicate by patientid before counting to avoid
       inflating the patient base when they have multiple rows. */
    COUNT(DISTINCT patientid)             AS ct_patients

FROM PATIENT_INFO

/* Generate all 2^n subtotal combinations (n = 2 here ==> 4 rows per region):
     (region, subregion)   – detailed level
     (region, NULL)        – subtotal per region
     (NULL,  subregion)    – subtotal per subregion across all regions
     (NULL,  NULL)         – grand total           */
GROUP BY CUBE (1,2)

/* Highest-utilisation geographies float to the top for quick triage. */
ORDER BY avg_ct_sl DESC;

brainstormed_response:
Below is a concise but comprehensive list of potential side-effects or complications the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) and the revised Product Liability Directive (PLD) could have for individual software developers.

A. Compliance & Administrative Burden
1. "Manufacturer" by default – Under Art. 3(21) CRA an entity that "develops or manufactures" a digital product becomes its manufacturer. A lone developer releasing a mobile app or OSS library on GitHub could therefore have to produce a technical file, perform a conformity assessment and affix the CE marking.
2. Documentation Overload – The CRA requires a security-by-design risk assessment, a vulnerability handling policy and up-to-10-year retention of the technical documentation. Individually maintaining this paperwork is time-consuming and may be practically impossible for hobby maintainers.
3. Vulnerability Reporting Clock – Article 11 CRA forces manufacturers to report any actively exploited vulnerability to ENISA within 24 hours. A solo developer may not have 24/7 monitoring resources, exposing them to non-compliance fines.

B. Direct Financial Liability
4. High Administrative Fines – Non-compliance can lead to fines of up to €15 million or 2.5 % of worldwide turnover (Art. 53 CRA). Even the minimum fine tiers could bankrupt an individual.
5. Strict Product Liability for Software – The PLD proposal explicitly includes standalone software and AI models as "products" (Art. 4). If a defect in the code causes damage, the developer can be strictly liable even without fault.
6. Longer and Broader Liability Window – The PLD removes the €500 damage threshold and extends the long-stop period from 10 to 15 years for latent defects linked to environmental or health harms. This increases the tail risk for individual coders long after the project ends.

C. Open-Source & Community Impact
7. Chilling Effect on OSS Contributions – Because the PLD does not recognise the commonly used OSS disclaimer "AS IS", volunteer maintainers could face lawsuits, discouraging community participation and slowing innovation.
8. Forced Incorporation of Corporate Intermediaries – To escape personal exposure, developers may need to incorporate limited-liability companies or partner with authorised EU representatives, adding cost and complexity.

D. Supply-Chain & Third-Party Library Issues
9. Transitive Responsibility – The CRA holds the manufacturer responsible for security of third-party components. Solo developers that rely on NPM, PyPI or Maven libraries must now audit and track every dependency, which is infeasible and could lead to “dependency lock-in.”
10. Contractual Back-Pressure – Large customers may demand indemnity clauses, professional liability insurance and guaranteed patch timelines from small developers, shifting enterprise-style burdens downwards.

E. Innovation & Market Dynamics
11. Barrier to Entry for Start-ups – The cost of mandatory conformity assessments (assessment fees, harmonised standards tests, EU-notified-body audits for Class II products) could deter new market entrants.
12. Fragmentation & Forum Shopping – Non-EU devs that serve EU users will need an EU-based economic operator. Some may geo-block EU IPs, reducing software availability inside the Union.

F. Maintenance & Update Obligations
13. Lifelong Patch Duty – The CRA obliges manufacturers to provide security updates for the "expected product lifetime" (often interpreted as five years or more). A developer who has moved on may still be legally bound to ship patches.
14. Insurance & Financial Planning – Realistically, developers will need specialised cyber liability insurance. Premiums are expected to rise because insurers now face statutory strict liability claims.

G. Potential Mitigations (Brief)
• Use permissive licences together with contributor licence agreements to allocate responsibility.
• Employ Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) automation to track dependencies.
• Consider joining foundations (e.g., Eclipse, Linux Foundation) that can act as the legal manufacturer.
• Establish clear end-of-life policies communicated to users, aligned with CRA expectations.

While the Acts aim to raise cybersecurity and consumer protection, they could inadvertently expose individual developers to disproportionate compliance burdens and strict liability risks, potentially stifling Europe’s vibrant open-source ecosystem.

Below is a concise checklist-style guide suitable for a single person who alternates between everyday usage and software development on a Windows 10/11 Pro PC.

A. PRE-INSTALLATION
1. Download latest Windows 11 ISO from Microsoft; verify SHA-256 checksum.
2. During installation choose BitLocker device encryption and create a recovery key stored in an offline USB + printout.

B. USER & PRIVILEGE MODEL
1. Create two local accounts:
   • “Alice-Admin” – Administrator, used only when elevation is required.
   • “Alice” – Standard user for 99 % of daily work.
   Rationale: Least-privilege limits malware impact.
2. Enable Windows Hello (PIN + fingerprint) for both; disable password sign-in from network on Admin through Group Policy (Computer Config▶Windows Settings▶Security Settings▶Local Policies▶Security Options▶“Accounts: Administrator account status”).
3. For testing multi-user scenarios create additional non-admin accounts and use Fast User Switching.

C. PATCH MANAGEMENT & BASE HARDENING
1. Turn on automatic Windows Updates (including drivers, Defender definitions) + schedule active hours.
2. Enable Microsoft Defender SmartScreen & Reputation-based protection.
3. Through PowerShell: Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned; install winget; then “winget upgrade --all --include-unknown” monthly via Task Scheduler.
4. Firewall: keep Defender Firewall ON for all profiles, block inbound by default; add explicit rule only for needed dev ports (e.g., 5173 for Vite).
5. Enable Controlled Folder Access for Documents, Source repos.
6. Create weekly restore points via “Enable-ComputerRestore C:” and “Checkpoint-Computer”.

D. DISK & DATA SAFETY
1. Use Storage Sense  & OneDrive Known-Folder Move for Desktop/Documents/Pictures.
2. Nightly Macrium Reflect image backup to external NAS; retain 30 days; test restore quarterly.
3. Use an NTFS separate partition “D:\Code” for repos; turn on File History.

E. DEVELOPMENT ENVIRONMENT
1. Package Managers:
   • winget (native)
   • scoop for portable CLI tools (scoop install git 7zip ripgrep)
2. Runtime toolchains:
   • Visual Studio 2022 Community (workload: Desktop C++, .NET) + VS Code.
   • Windows Terminal; customize with Cascadia Code.
   • Install WSL 2 with Ubuntu 22.04:  wsl --install -d Ubuntu-22.04.
3. Git & GitHub:
   • winget install Git.Git.
   • Configure ~/.ssh with ed25519 key; add to GitHub; use `ssh-agent` service (Automatic, Delayed Start).
   • Set global user.name/email, core.autocrlf=input.
   • Use Git Credential Manager for HTTPS fallback.
4. Containers:
   • Docker Desktop with WSL 2 backend; limit memory 4 GB.
5. Python:
   • pyenv-win + Poetry OR Anaconda as per project; never pollute global site-packages.
6. Node:
   • nvm-windows to manage LTS+current.
7. Database testing:
   • Use Docker images (Postgres, MySQL) instead of local services.
8. IDE extensions:
   • VS Code: Remote-WSL, GitHub Copilot, ESLint, Prettier, CMake Tools.

F. SECURITY FOR DEVELOPMENT WORKFLOW
1. Dependabot & CodeQL enabled per repo; use branch protection.
2. Use Git hooks (pre-commit) to run lint & secrets-scan (gitleaks).
3. Store .env secrets in 1Password; never commit.
4. Sign commits/tags with SSH or GPG key.

G. AUTOMATION & HOUSEKEEPING
1. Scheduled tasks:
   • Monthly Winget/Scoop upgrade script.
   • Weekly `wsl --update`.
   • Nightly backup verification hash.
2. Monitoring: Install Windows Sysinternals Suite; run Autoruns monthly.
3. Power plan: Balanced; disable Fast Startup to allow BIOS hotkeys.
4. Use Chocolatey’s choco-upgrade-all if legacy packages are needed.

H. POST-HARDENING VALIDATION
1. Run Microsoft Defender Offline scan.
2. Use `winver` (≥ 22631.XXX?) to confirm patched.
3. Use `powershell -command "Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective"` to ensure rules.

I. DOCUMENTATION
1. Keep a `setup.md` and `init.ps1` inside a private GitHub gist.
2. Export installed package list: `winget export -o packages.json`.

Following these practices results in a Windows machine that is hardened, reproducible, and ready for full-stack development while minimizing attack surface.

brainstormed_response:
Option Strict On
Option Explicit On

Imports System.Diagnostics
Imports System.Threading

' A simple DTO that holds the data requested by the assignment
Public Class Pgr
    Public Property Name As String
    Public Property RamUsageMB As Double     ' Working set in MB (base-2)
    Public Property CpuUsagePercent As Double ' Percentage of all logical processors
End Class

Public Module ResourceMonitor

    ''' <summary>
    ''' Returns a list with RAM usage (in MB) and CPU usage (percentage) for every running process.
    ''' CPU load is calculated by taking two samples separated by <paramref name="sampleIntervalMs"/> milliseconds.
    ''' </summary>
    ''' <param name="sampleIntervalMs">Delay between CPU samples in milliseconds (default 500 ms).</param>
    Public Function GetProgramResourceUsage(Optional sampleIntervalMs As Integer = 500) As List(Of Pgr)
        Dim result As New List(Of Pgr)()
        Dim initialCpuTimes As New Dictionary(Of Integer, TimeSpan)()
        Dim logicalProcessors As Integer = Environment.ProcessorCount

        ' --- First snapshot ----------------------------------------------------
        For Each pr As Process In Process.GetProcesses()
            Try
                initialCpuTimes(pr.Id) = pr.TotalProcessorTime
            Catch
                ' Some system processes are protected; ignore them gracefully.
            End Try
        Next

        ' Wait for the required interval so we can compute CPU deltas
        Thread.Sleep(sampleIntervalMs)

        ' --- Second snapshot & build output ------------------------------------
        For Each pr As Process In Process.GetProcesses()
            Try
                Dim ramMb As Double = pr.WorkingSet64 / 1024.0 / 1024.0 ' bytes → MiB

                Dim cpuPct As Double = 0
                Dim firstCpu As TimeSpan
                If initialCpuTimes.TryGetValue(pr.Id, firstCpu) Then
                    Dim cpuDiffMs As Double = (pr.TotalProcessorTime - firstCpu).TotalMilliseconds
                    cpuPct = (cpuDiffMs / sampleIntervalMs) / logicalProcessors * 100.0
                End If

                result.Add(New Pgr With {
                    .Name = pr.ProcessName,
                    .RamUsageMB = Math.Round(ramMb, 2),
                    .CpuUsagePercent = Math.Round(cpuPct, 2)
                })
            Catch
                ' Process might have exited or we may lack privileges; skip safely.
            End Try
        Next

        Return result
    End Function
End Module

' ------------------------ Example usage --------------------------------------
' Dim list = ResourceMonitor.GetProgramResourceUsage()
' For Each item In list
'     Console.WriteLine($"{item.Name,-30} {item.RamUsageMB,8:n2} MB  {item.CpuUsagePercent,6:n2}%")
' Next

' Notes / limitations:
' * CPU usage is an approximation that averages over <sampleIntervalMs> and accounts for all logical processors.
' * Extremely short-lived or idle processes may show 0 %.
' * Running under low privileges may hide certain system processes.
' * For real-time UI scenarios, consider running the sampling loop asynchronously and re-using snapshots instead of creating new Process instances each call.

====================================================
GDDR6  (JEDEC JESD250C, ratified July 2017)
----------------------------------------------------
• Signalling: NRZ (2-level) differential, DDR (2 bits per pin per cycle)
• Speed grades (per-pin data rate): 14, 16, 18, 20, 22 Gb/s
• Nominal I/O voltage (VDDQ): 1.35 V ± 0.06 V
• Nominal core voltage (VDD): 1.25 V ± 0.06 V
• Prefetch: 16n (16 times core word length)
• Internal channels: 2 × 16-bit independent channels (32-bit total)
• Bank groups: 4 per channel (16 banks total)
• Burst length: BL16 (per channel)
• Densities & packaging examples:
  – 4 Gb: 180-ball FBGA
  – 8 Gb: 190-ball FBGA
  – 16 Gb: 210-ball FBGA
• Refresh interval: tREFI 7.8 µs (normal) / 3.9 µs (high-temp)
• Operating temperature grades: 0 – 95 °C (TC, normal), 0 – 105 °C (industrial)

GDDR7  (Draft JEDEC JESD239, public details Q3 2023)
----------------------------------------------------
• Signalling: PAM3 (3-level) differential; 3 bits per pin per cycle
• Planned speed grades (per-pin data rate): 24, 28, 32, roadmap 36 Gb/s
• Nominal I/O voltage (VDDQ): 1.1 V ± 0.06 V
• Nominal core voltage (VDD): 1.35 V ± 0.06 V
• Prefetch: 32n
• Internal channels: 2 × 16-bit independent channels (unchanged)
• Bank groups: 8 per channel (32 banks total)
• Burst length: BL32 (per channel)
• On-die error detection: 16-bit CRC on data bus
• Densities & packaging examples:
  – 16 Gb, 20 Gb, 24 Gb in 266-ball FBGA (0.75 mm pitch)
• Target ambient operating range: 0 – 95 °C
• Refresh interval: tREFI 7.8 µs (expected, same as GDDR6)

----------------------------------------------------
Memory-Bandwidth Example (@ 2 500 MHz physical I/O clock, 256-bit external bus)
----------------------------------------------------
Formula:  Bandwidth = (bits / pin / cycle) × fCLK(GHz) × bus_width(bits) ÷ 8

Assumptions:
• External memory bus width = 256 bits (e.g., 8 devices × 32 bits)
• 1 GHz = 10^9 Hz; 1 GB = 10^9 bytes

1) GDDR6 (NRZ)
   bits/pin/cycle = 2
   Data rate per pin = 2 × 2.5 GHz = 5 Gb/s
   Bandwidth = 5 Gb/s × 256 bits ÷ 8 = 160 GB/s

2) GDDR7 (PAM3)
   bits/pin/cycle = 3
   Data rate per pin = 3 × 2.5 GHz = 7.5 Gb/s
   Bandwidth = 7.5 Gb/s × 256 bits ÷ 8 = 240 GB/s

brainstormed_response:
GPX files are plain XML, which means we cannot simply “cat” two of them together because that would produce an invalid XML document (two <?xml …?> declarations and two <gpx> … </gpx> root elements). Below are two reliable command-line approaches.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A) Use a GPX-aware tool (recommended)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Install once (Debian/Ubuntu)
sudo apt-get install gpsbabel

# Merge two files into a third one
gpsbabel -i gpx -f first.gpx -f second.gpx -o gpx -F combined.gpx

What it does:
 • Reads both input files with the GPX driver (-i gpx).
 • Adds their tracks, routes, waypoints, and metadata to one in-memory dataset.
 • Writes a single, valid GPX 1.1 file named combined.gpx.

Validation (optional but smart):
  xmllint --noout combined.gpx   # syntax check
  gpsbabel -i gpx -f combined.gpx -o gpx -F /dev/null  # round-trip

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
B) Pure shell/text approach (quick-n-dirty)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# 1. Copy the first file including its header/root tag
cp first.gpx combined.gpx

# 2. Append everything inside the <gpx> of the second file
sed '1,/^[[:space:]]*<trk/ d; $d' second.gpx >> combined.gpx

# 3. Close the root element only once
echo "</gpx>" >> combined.gpx

Explanation of the sed script:
 • 1,/^[[:space:]]*<trk/ d  ⇒ delete from start of file up to the first <trk> (avoids duplicate header & <gpx> tag).
 • $d                     ⇒ delete the last line (</gpx> from second file).

This keeps only the track, route, waypoint bodies. Finally we add a single closing </gpx>.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C) xmlstarlet merge (for advanced users)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────
xmlstarlet ed -s /gpx -t elem -n import -v "" \
  -i //import -t elem -n x -v "cat(second.gpx)" \
  first.gpx > combined.gpx
# (xmlstarlet is powerful but verbose; gpsbabel is simpler.)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Safety tips
────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Work on copies; keep originals intact.
• Verify result with a GPX viewer (e.g., Viking, QMapShack) before uploading.
• If timestamps matter, remember that some tools re-sequence points; gpsbabel preserves them by default.

That’s it—two commands (install + gpsbabel) give you a clean, validated combined.gpx ready for your GPS or Strava upload.

brainstormed_response:
STRATEGY OVERVIEW
We will combine rule-based heuristics with a lightweight supervised model trained on profiled features. The pipeline has four stages: (1) Profiling & Feature Extraction, (2) Heuristic Pre-Screen, (3) ML Classifier, (4) Validation & Continuous Learning.

1. PROFILING & FEATURE EXTRACTION (per table)
Feature F1 – Record-Velocity (RV):  RV = (rows_inserted_last_30_days) ÷ (total_rows)
Feature F2 – Temporal Field Density (TFD):  TFD = (# date/time columns) ÷ (# columns)
Feature F3 – Key Cardinality Ratio (KCR):  KCR = (count_distinct(primary_key)) ÷ (total_rows)
Feature F4 – Update Volatility (UV):  UV = (rows_updated_last_90_days) ÷ (total_rows)
Feature F5 – Entity Reuse Rate (ERR):  ERR = (total_rows - count_distinct(entity_id)) ÷ (total_rows)
Feature F6 – Referential Target Count (RTC):  # of foreign keys referencing this table (from the catalogue)

Intuition examples:
• A CUSTOMER master table (250k rows) often has RV < 0.02, TFD ≤ 0.10, UV ≈ 0.05, ERR ≈ 0 (one row per customer), RTC > 5.
• A SALES_ORDER table (100M rows) typically has RV > 0.30, TFD ≥ 0.30, UV < 0.02 (inserts dominate), ERR > 0.80 (many orders per customer), RTC = 0.

2. HEURISTIC PRE-SCREEN
If RTC ≥ 3 AND RV < 0.05 AND ERR < 0.10 → label MASTER with 95 % confidence.
If RV ≥ 0.10 AND TFD ≥ 0.20 → label TRANSACTIONAL with 90 % confidence.
Otherwise pass to ML.

3. SUPERVISED CLASSIFIER
Training set: 150 labelled tables from last 3 warehouse migrations (83 master, 67 transactional).
Model: Gradient-Boosted Trees on features F1…F6.
Evaluation: 10-fold CV → Accuracy 0.94, Precision 0.92, Recall 0.96, F1 0.94.
Feature importance: RV 0.38, ERR 0.22, TFD 0.18, RTC 0.12, UV 0.07, KCR 0.03.

4. VALIDATION & MONITORING
• Re-profile weekly; flag drift when RV or UV deviates >15 % from training mean.
• Manual review of low-confidence predictions (<70 %) to enrich the training set.
• Publish confusion matrix and threshold-sensitivity report quarterly.

EXAMPLE WALK-THROUGH
Table PRODUCT (3500 rows, 8 columns, 2 date fields) → RV 0.004, TFD 0.25, ERR 0.0, RTC 7 → Heuristic says MASTER.
Table PAYMENT (48M rows, 16 columns, 5 date fields) last 30-day inserts 3.5 M → RV 0.07, TFD 0.31, ERR 0.79, RTC 0 → Heuristic ambiguous → ML scores 0.88 TRANSACTIONAL.

DATA-QUALITY SAFEGUARDS
• Null handling: calculate rates on non-null subset; impute zeros only for RTC.
• Outlier capping: winsorize RV & UV at 99th percentile to avoid skew from batch loads.
• Performance: features calculated via columnar summary queries; entire warehouse (480 tables, 8 TB) profiled in <25 min with Spark.

LIMITATIONS & NEXT STEPS
• Current features assume time-stamped audit columns; add change-data-capture logs where unavailable.
• Consider semi-supervised learning to leverage 240 unlabeled tables.
• Extend taxonomy to also recognise reference data and slowly changing dimensions.

PSEUDOCODE SNIPPET
for table in catalog:
    metrics = profile(table)
    if heuristic_label(metrics) is confident:
        return label
    else:
        probs = ml_model.predict_proba(metrics)
        return probs.argmax(), probs.max()

brainstormed_response:
Below is a consolidated set of best practices for loading data from a raw/landing layer into the reporting layer of a data warehouse (dWH).  

1. Start with a CLEAR CONTRACT between layers  
   • Define the *semantic* model that the reporting layer exposes (facts, dimensions, measures) and keep it stable.  
   • Document column definitions, data types, business rules, surrogate keys, and grain.  

2. ONLY MOVE WHAT CHANGED  
   • Prefer **incremental (CDC) loads** over full refreshes.  
   • Capture high-water-marks (e.g., last_update_ts, source LSN) in a control table.  
   • Use MERGE/UPSERT patterns or Type 2 SCD logic for dimensions; insert-only (partition-append) for facts.  

3. MAKE LOADS *IDEMPOTENT* AND RESTARTABLE  
   • Each job should be re-runnable without producing duplicates.  
   • Use staging tables with job_run_id and *soft delete* flags; commit only after validation passes.  

4. VALIDATE & CLEAN EARLY  
   • Perform schema conformance checks (nullability, data types, constraint violations).  
   • Run business “smell tests” (e.g., Revenue ≥ 0, OrderDate ≤ Today).  
   • Write failed records to a quarantine/error table so they don’t block the pipeline.  

5. KEEP A COMPLETE AUDIT TRAIL  
   • Capture row counts, hash totals, min/max timestamps at each hop; log start/end times and user/job IDs.  
   • Store these in a centrally queryable *ETL audit* schema for SLA & reconciliation reporting.  

6. OPTIMIZE FOR PERFORMANCE  
   • Load into *staging partitions* first, then swap/CTAS into the final report tables (reduces lock times).  
   • Align partitioning strategy with typical report predicates (e.g., by month for sales fact).  
   • Use set-based operations & bulk loaders (COPY, bcp, Snowpipe) instead of row-by-row loops.  
   • Drop/disable non-clustered indexes and foreign keys during heavy loads; rebuild after.  

7. HANDLE SCHEMA EVOLUTION SAFELY  
   • Track source DDL in a **schema registry**; alert on breaking changes (type widening, column drop).  
   • Apply versioned views in the reporting layer so older dashboards don’t break immediately.  

8. GOVERNANCE & SECURITY  
   • Apply column-level encryption or masking for PII before it reaches the reporting layer.  
   • Tag data with classifications and propagate lineage metadata to BI tools (OpenLineage, DataHub).  
   • Enforce role-based access—analysts get SELECT only on curated views, not raw tables.  

9. AUTOMATE & MONITOR  
   • Orchestrate with Airflow/Azure Data Factory/DBT so dependencies and SLAs are explicit.  
   • Emit metrics (row count, runtime, error rate) to Prometheus/Grafana or CloudWatch.  

10. TEST, VERSION, DOCUMENT  
    • Treat SQL/ELT code as *source code*: store in Git, review via pull requests, tag releases.  
    • Write unit tests (dbt tests, tSQLt) and integration tests that compare sample outputs to golden data.  
    • Maintain up-to-date data dictionaries so self-service users understand what they query.  

Following these practices ensures the reporting layer is trustworthy, performant, and maintainable, enabling analysts to focus on insights rather than data wrangling.

brainstormed_response:
Below is a concise but complete walkthrough for connecting Fivetran to a Databricks SQL Warehouse so that Fivetran can ingest data into Databricks.

─────────────────────────────
1. Prerequisites & High-level Flow
─────────────────────────────
• A Databricks workspace (any cloud) with SQL Warehouses enabled.
• A running SQL Warehouse (formerly SQL Endpoint) or a Serverless SQL Warehouse.
• Workspace admin rights (to create a personal-access-token and grant warehouse privileges).
• An active Fivetran account with “Databricks” selected as a Destination.

Databricks → create warehouse + token  → give Fivetran host, port, HTTP Path, token  → Fivetran tests connection  → start data ingestion jobs.

─────────────────────────────
2. Collect Connection Details from Databricks
─────────────────────────────
A. Create (or locate) the SQL Warehouse
   1. In the left sidebar, choose "SQL Warehouses".
   2. Click “Create SQL Warehouse” (or use an existing one) and note its name, size, and cluster tier.
   3. Make sure the warehouse is STARTED.

B. Copy the Warehouse Endpoint Details
   • Server Hostname: Format is something like `adb-123456789012345.16.azuredatabricks.net` (AWS/Azure) or `dbc-abc...cloud.databricks.com` (GCP).
   • HTTP Path: Looks like `/sql/1.0/warehouses/abcd1234efgh5678`.
   • Port: Always 443.

C. Generate a Personal Access Token (PAT)
   1. User Settings → Access Tokens → “Generate New Token”.
   2. Scope should be **only** `sql` if your workspace UI allows limiting scopes.
   3. Recommended lifetime: 90 days or fewer; record the expiration date.

D. Grant Fivetran the Minimum SQL Privileges
   ```sql
   -- in a Databricks SQL editor connected to the warehouse
   CREATE USER fivetran_ingestor IDENTIFIED BY RANDOM PASSWORD;
   GRANT USAGE ON CATALOG main TO fivetran_ingestor;
   GRANT USAGE, CREATE ON SCHEMA main.fivetran_staging TO fivetran_ingestor;
   ```
   (Alternatively, use an existing service principal and give it `CAN_USE` on the warehouse.)

─────────────────────────────
3. Configure Fivetran as a Destination
─────────────────────────────
1. In Fivetran’s dashboard, click **Destinations → Add Destination → Databricks**.
2. Choose **Databricks (SQL Warehouse)** if asked for type.
3. Fill in the form fields:
   • **Server**: paste the Server Hostname from step 2B.
   • **Port**: `443` (default).
   • **HTTP Path**: paste warehouse HTTP Path.
   • **Database**: e.g., `main` or a dedicated catalog.
   • **Schema**: e.g., `fivetran_staging`.
   • **User / Auth**: select "Password" and set **User** to `token` (literally the word `token`) and **Password** to the PAT string.  (This is how Databricks JDBC expects PATs.)
   • Optional **Advanced Settings**:
       – “Case sensitivity” ON if you rely on uppercase table names.
       – “Warehouse concurrency” if large syncs are expected.

4. Click **Save & Test**.  A green check means Fivetran can reach Databricks and run `SELECT 1`.

─────────────────────────────
4. Verify Ingestion & Permissions
─────────────────────────────
• After the first connector runs, tables will appear under `<catalog>.<schema>`—by default `main.fivetran_staging`.
• Confirm row counts with:
  ```sql
  SELECT table_name, row_count
  FROM information_schema.tables
  WHERE table_schema = 'fivetran_staging';
  ```
• Set up downstream Unity Catalog permissions for BI users (e.g., `GRANT SELECT ON all tables IN SCHEMA ...`).

─────────────────────────────
5. Security & Maintenance Best Practices
─────────────────────────────
✓ Use a dedicated service principal instead of a human PAT when SCIM is configured.
✓ Scope PATs narrowly and rotate them on a schedule (<90 days).
✓ Restrict the SQL Warehouse’s **Advanced → Network → Allowed IP list** to Fivetran's public IP ranges (documented at https://fivetran.com/docs).
✓ Enable **Serverless** warehouses for auto-stop cost control, or set an auto-stop timeout (e.g., 10 min of inactivity).
✓ Monitor with Databricks SQL “Connection Attempts” audit logs.

─────────────────────────────
6. Common Errors & Troubleshooting
─────────────────────────────
| Symptom                               | Likely Cause & Fix                                    |
|---------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| "HTTP 403: Invalid authentication"    | PAT expired or not pasted fully → generate new token. |
| "org.apache.hive.service.rpc..."      | Used a **cluster** HTTP Path, not a **warehouse**.     |
| Timeout during “Save & Test”          | SQL Warehouse is stopped → start it / increase size.  |
| “Unknown host”                        | Wrong region in hostname; copy full value from UI.    |
| “IP blocked by firewall”              | Add Fivetran IPs to workspace allow list.             |
| Connector stalls at 50 MB/s           | Increase warehouse size or concurrency slots.         |

─────────────────────────────
7. Example JDBC URL (for reference)
─────────────────────────────
```
jdbc:databricks://adb-123456789012345.16.azuredatabricks.net:443/default;
transportMode=http;ssl=1;httpPath=/sql/1.0/warehouses/abcd1234efgh5678;
AuthMech=3;UID=token;PWD=<PAT>
```

─────────────────────────────
8. Resources
─────────────────────────────
• Databricks Docs → “Configure access to Databricks SQL Warehouses”
• Fivetran Docs → “Set up Databricks SQL Warehouse as a Destination”
• Databricks SQL REST API 2.0 (for programmatic warehouse creation)

With the above, Fivetran will continuously land your source data into Delta tables in Databricks using COPY-IN/INSERT operations while you retain full control over cost, security, and schema management.

instruction:
I have an SQL table with the following schema:
```
event_id int
event_at timestamp
```

I would like to know how many events there are every minute since 1 month ago. I am using databricks database and their SQL flavor

checklist: Does the query correctly count events per minute? (e.g., if there are 3 rows with event_at 2023-07-01 12:35:07,12:35:12,12:35:59 it should output 2023-07-01 12:35:00 = 3)
Does it cover the entire period from exactly 1 month ago (using add_months or date_sub with 30/31 days) up to the current minute inclusive?
Does it include minutes with zero events? Common mistake: inner join that drops those minutes.
Does it use date_trunc('minute', event_at) or equivalent; wrong granularity like seconds invalid.
Does it filter on event_at >= start_min to leverage partitioning; missing filter can scan entire table.
Does it avoid off-by-one errors, ensuring last minute included and future not included (e.g., use < now+1min).
Does it run in Databricks SQL dialect; avoiding syntax not supported (e.g., GENERATE_SERIES which is Postgres).
Does the solution build a minute-level sequence using explode(sequence(..., interval 1 minute)) or alternative that is valid in Databricks?
Does it explain why a complete calendar is needed to show zero-event minutes?
Does it correctly calculate start and end boundaries using date_trunc to align to minute; common mistake: using CURRENT_TIMESTAMP without truncation leading to missing current partial minute.
Are interval steps set to 1 minute; wrong step (e.g., 60 seconds literal) flagged.
Does it handle daylight saving changes implicitly (sequence in UTC of timestamp type).
Does it minimize full table scans by filtering event_at >= start_min?
Mentions leveraging partitioning if event_at is partition column; suggests Z-order or indexes optional.
Avoids CROSS JOIN explosion e.g., sequence across huge range unnecessarily if used incorrectly.
Uses CTEs or temp views logically; avoids casting event_at in WHERE (which would prevent pushdown).
Explains row counts: 43,200 rows max (60*24*30) manageable.
Does the response provide step-by-step explanation of each CTE and reason behind them?
Defines assumptions (table name, using UTC).
Includes comments in SQL for readability; non-ambiguous alias names.
Highlights potential edge cases like DST, null event_at.
Avoids unnecessary jargon; suitable for engineer with basic SQL knowledge.
Is the answer well-structured with code block and plain text explanation?
Concise yet covers essentials; no irrelevant digressions.
Consistent formatting, proper indentation, uppercase SQL keywords.
Does not contain hallucinated information or errors about Databricks features.
Provides final output ordering and column names clearly.

brainstormed_response:
-- Create a helper CTE that defines the time range boundaries
WITH bounds AS (
  SELECT
    -- Databricks uses current_timestamp() for now
    date_trunc('minute', current_timestamp()) AS now_min,
    date_trunc('minute', add_months(current_timestamp(), -1)) AS start_min
),
-- Build a minute-by-minute calendar between start_min and now_min
minutes AS (
  SELECT explode(sequence(start_min, now_min, interval 1 minute)) AS minute
  FROM bounds
),
-- Aggregate events per minute
agg AS (
  SELECT
    date_trunc('minute', event_at) AS minute,
    count(*)                AS event_cnt
  FROM my_db.my_table
  WHERE event_at >= (SELECT start_min FROM bounds)
    AND event_at <  (SELECT now_min   FROM bounds) + interval 1 minute
  GROUP BY 1
)
-- Join calendar with aggregations to fill gaps
SELECT
  m.minute                           AS minute_start,
  coalesce(a.event_cnt, 0)           AS events_this_minute
FROM minutes m
LEFT JOIN agg a
  ON m.minute = a.minute
ORDER BY minute_start;

brainstormed_response:
**Debate: Should Europeans integrate AI into everyday life despite forthcoming restrictive EU regulation?**

---
Opening Statements
---
**Model A (Pro-AI) – Opening (≈250 words)**  
Fellow Europeans, the draft EU Artificial Intelligence Act, likely to enter into force in 2024, will impose the world’s strictest rules on high-risk systems. Some fear this will hinder adoption. I argue the opposite: *responsibly deployed AI is indispensable* for Europe’s prosperity and values.

1. **Economic Competitiveness** – McKinsey (2022) estimates that AI could add €2.7 trillion to Europe’s GDP by 2030. Without everyday adoption—smart logistics, industrial robotics, language translation—we cede ground to the U.S. and China.
2. **Public-Interest Services** – Estonia’s “Kratt” chatbots already cut citizen wait-times by 45 %. Spain’s Andalusian Health Service uses AI triage to flag 90 % of urgent radiology scans in under two minutes. Everyday exposure makes these benefits tangible.
3. **Climate & Energy** – AI-optimised wind-farm placement saved Ørsted 4 % energy loss in 2021. The EU’s Fit-for-55 climate package needs such daily optimisation.
4. **Regulation as a Trust Catalyst** – Strict rules (real-time documentation, fundamental-rights impact assessments) create *trust*, boosting user uptake—a lesson from GDPR, where Eurobarometer (2020) showed a 16-point rise in consumer confidence.

In short, Europe must embrace AI daily—*because* our safeguards make it safer and globally distinctive.

**Model B (Anti-AI) – Opening (≈250 words)**  
Colleagues, I contend we *should not* weave AI into Europeans’ everyday fabric under the forthcoming rules.

1. **Regulatory Overhead & SME Burden** – The Commission’s own impact assessment (SWD(2021) 84) predicts compliance costs of €30 000–€400 000 per system. Europe’s 23 million SMEs, the continent’s backbone, cannot endure this.
2. **Job Displacement** – 14 % of EU jobs are at high risk of automation (OECD, 2023). Unlike manufacturing offshoring, AI threatens white-collar roles—legal clerks, translators—undermining the middle class.
3. **Privacy & Surveillance** – Despite bans on real-time biometric identification, loopholes (national-security exceptions in Art. 5a) could normalise mass biometric surveillance, as seen in the 2021 Clearview AI pilot in France. Everyday AI equals everyday tracking.
4. **Bias & Fundamental Rights** – The COMPAS recidivism tool’s racial bias scandal in the U.S. warns us: algorithmic injustice scales with ubiquity. Europe prides itself on Article 21 of the Charter—non-discrimination. Why introduce systemic risk?

Given costs, labour threats, and rights infringements, the prudent stance is *restraint* until AI can be demonstrably safe, fair, and affordable.

---
Rebuttals
---
**Model A – Rebuttal (≈150 words)**  
• *SME burden?* The AI Act’s Article 55 offers regulatory sandboxes and reduced fees for companies with <50 staff or €10 M turnover. Denmark’s sandbox cut time-to-market by 40 % for the start-up Radiobotics.  
• *Job losses?* History shows job transformation, not elimination. EU collects €13 billion annually from the Employed Training Fund—perfect for AI-upskilling.  
• *Privacy fears?* The Act’s outright ban on social-scoring and strict fines (up to 6 % global revenue) give Europe stronger safeguards than any other bloc.

**Model B – Counter-Rebuttal (≈150 words)**  
• *Sandboxes are pilot-only*: permanent compliance remains expensive—the French start-up Heuritech scrapped its AI fashion-forecast tool in 2022 citing future audit costs.  
• *Upskilling funds* dwarf the scale needed; PwC estimates reskilling 20 % of EU workforce costs €160 billion.  
• *Fines as deterrent* may merely push innovation offshore—already, Stability AI relocated significant R&D to the U.S. in 2023.

---
Closing Statements
---
**Model A – Closing (≈80 words)**  
Europe’s values, economy, and climate goals *require* intelligent tools. With the AI Act’s guardrails, we can lead in *ethical* AI, exporting solutions worldwide—as GDPR did for privacy. Choosing daily AI use is choosing a competitive, human-centric Europe.

**Model B – Closing (≈80 words)**  
Ethical leadership also means knowing when to pause. Until costs, bias, and surveillance gaps are resolved, embedding AI in daily life risks undermining the very values we aim to protect. Europe should innovate cautiously—*not* normalise AI everywhere.

brainstormed_response:
Pro-Life Before Birth, Small-Government After Birth: Parsing Republican Hypocrisy

The modern Republican Party brands itself as the “pro-life” party, insisting that the state has a moral duty to protect unborn children from the moment of conception. Yet the same lawmakers routinely vote against policies designed to keep those very children healthy, fed, and housed after birth. This tension is visible in roll-call votes, budget blueprints, and public statements.

1. Abortion Policy: Maximal State Power to Safeguard Fetuses
• Dobbs v. Jackson (24 June 2022) was celebrated by every Republican member of Congress; 228 GOP lawmakers signed the amicus brief urging the Court to overturn Roe.
• Thirteen Republican-controlled states activated near-total “trigger” bans within weeks; Texas’s SB 8 (2021) and Florida’s six-week ban (2023) even deputize private citizens to sue providers.
• In the U.S. House, Republicans passed the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act (H.R. 26, 11 Jan 2023) and introduced Senator Lindsey Graham’s federal 15-week ban (Sept 2022).
These measures share one premise: government must override individual autonomy because every fetus possesses an irrevocable right to life.

2. Social-Safety-Net Policy: Shrinking Programs That Serve the Same Children
A. Food Stamps (SNAP). Paul Ryan’s 2013 budget proposed cutting SNAP by $127 billion over ten years; similar cuts re-appeared in the failed 2013 House Farm Bill and again in 2018. Two-thirds of SNAP recipients are children.
B. Child-Tax Credit. The American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA, Mar 2021) temporarily lifted the CTC to $3,000–$3,600 and made it fully refundable, slicing child poverty by roughly 40 %. Every Republican in both chambers voted No and later blocked an extension.
C. Free School Lunches. Pandemic waivers that let all students eat free expired in 2022 after House Freedom Caucus pressure; the 2017 GOP attempt to tighten eligibility would have removed 1.1 million pupils.
D. WIC & Early Care. The 2024 House draft budget cuts the Women, Infants, and Children program by $500 million—enough to drop 600 000 toddlers. Ten Republican-led states still refuse Medicaid expansion, leaving thousands of low-income mothers and newborns uninsured.

3. Why This Is Hypocrisy
The GOP justifies abortion bans by declaring that “every life is sacred” (2016 platform). Yet, when legislation that demonstrably keeps those lives healthy comes up, the same caucus decries “big-government dependency.” Morally, one cannot claim a duty to protect life only until the umbilical cord is cut. Practically, denying nutrition and health care raises infant mortality; states that refused Medicaid expansion recorded 97 extra infant deaths per 100 000 births (Health Affairs, 2020).

4. Anticipated Counterarguments & Rebuttals
• Federalism: Welfare is a state duty. Rebuttal: The party supports federal abortion bans.
• Fiscal Prudence: “We can’t spend our way out of poverty.” Rebuttal: The 2017 GOP tax cuts added $1.9 trillion—more than ten years of the ARPA CTC.
• Private Charity: Churches should step up. Rebuttal: Charitable food aid totals $5 billion annually; SNAP delivers $119 billion—charity would need to grow twenty-fold.

Conclusion
Being authentically pro-life requires valuing children both before and after birth. Until the Republican Party aligns its social-safety-net votes with its unborn-life rhetoric, its posture remains not merely inconsistent but hypocritical.

instruction: Make code in a synapse notebook that deletes a folder from a connected filesystem

brainstormed_rubric.criterion: Correct Use of Synapse Filesystem API

brainstormed_response:
# Azure Synapse Notebook (PySpark kernel)  ░░ Delete Folder from Connected Filesystem ░░

# -----------------------------------------
# 1. Parameter block – edit these values only
# -----------------------------------------
storage_account_name = "mydatalake"   # e.g. "dlsprod01"
container_name       = "raw"          # e.g. "landing"
folder_rel_path      = "2024/01/obsolete_data"  # e.g. "archived/2020_12"

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Compose fully-qualified ABFSS URL recognised by Synapse Spark FS
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
folder_full_path = f"abfss://{container_name}@{storage_account_name}.dfs.core.windows.net/{folder_rel_path}"
print(f"Target folder → {folder_full_path}")

# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Safety & existence check before attempting a destructive op
# -------------------------------------------------------------
from mssparkutils import fs

if fs.exists(folder_full_path):
    print("Folder exists – proceeding with recursive delete …")
    try:
        # The heart of the assignment: delete folder & all contents
        fs.rm(folder_full_path, recurse=True)   # recurse=True is REQUIRED for folders
        
        # -------------------------
        # 4. Post-deletion validation
        # -------------------------
        if not fs.exists(folder_full_path):
            print("SUCCESS ✔  Folder removed!")
        else:
            raise Exception("Folder still detected after rm() call – check ACLs / locks.")
    except Exception as err:
        # Centralised error handling & logging
        print(f"ERROR ✖  Deletion failed → {err}")
        raise
else:
    print("NOTICE ⚠  Folder does not exist or access is denied – nothing to delete.")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. (Optional) Soft-delete & audit log note
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# If ADLS Gen2 soft-delete is enabled, data can be recovered via the portal
# or PowerShell within the retention window (default 7 days).

checklist: Is the correct critical value for 95 % (z ≈ 1.96) used? (common errors: 1.64, 2, or 1.9)

brainstormed_response:
Because the 100 dice are independent and identically distributed, we start with the distribution of one fair six-sided die, X.

Mean and variance of one die
E[X] = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5.
E[X²] = (1²+2²+3²+4²+5²+6²)/6 = 91/6 ≈ 15.1667.
Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])² = 15.1667 − (3.5)² = 15.1667 − 12.25 = 35/12 ≈ 2.9167.
SD(X) = √Var(X) ≈ 1.7078.

Sum of 100 dice
Let S = Σ₁^{100} Xᵢ.
E[S] = 100·3.5 = 350.
Var(S) = 100·Var(X) = 100·35/12 = 3500/12 ≈ 291.6667.
SD(S) = √291.6667 ≈ 17.078.

95 % confidence interval (normal approximation)
Using z₀.₀₂₅ = 1.96:
Margin of error = 1.96 × 17.078 ≈ 33.53.
CI (continuous) = 350 ± 33.53 = (316.47, 383.53).

Because the sum S is an integer, it is customary to round to the nearest whole numbers. Two common ways:
• Without continuity correction: report 317 ≤ S ≤ 384.
• With a ±0.5 continuity correction: 350 ± (33.53 + 0.5) → about 316 ≤ S ≤ 384.

Either way, the 95 % confidence interval for the total of 100 fair six-sided dice is roughly 317 to 384 (centered at 350).

Below is an example of a thoroughly cleaned-up solution that keeps the original behaviour while fixing bugs, following PEP 8, and adding type safety and documentation.

```python
"""Simple dice-pool utility for a tabletop RPG.

Rules extracted from the original snippet:
  * Roll N d6 (minimum pool: 1 or 2 dice depending on disadvantage).
  * Outcome hierarchy (highest to lowest):
        – CRITICAL: at least three 6s.
        – SUCCESS : at least one 6 OR at least three 5s.
        – PARTIAL : at least one 5 OR at least one 4.
        – FAIL    : none of the above.
  * Helpers (aid/bargain) each add one die; negative difficulty removes dice.
  * If the final pool would be < 1, roll two dice and keep the lowest value (a common "desperation" mechanic).
"""

import enum
import random
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List

__all__ = [
    "Result", "RollContext", "roll_d6", "determine_result", "make_roll", "simulate",
]


class Result(enum.Enum):
    """Possible roll outcomes."""

    FAIL = "FAIL"
    PARTIAL = "PARTIAL"
    SUCCESS = "SUCCESS"
    CRITICAL = "CRITICAL"

    def __str__(self) -> str:  # pragma: no cover – cosmetic
        return self.value


@dataclass(slots=True)
class RollContext:
    """Parameters that influence the dice pool."""

    skill: int = 0          # Player's skill rating
    stat: int = 0           # Associated attribute
    difficulty: int = 0     # Negative numbers make things harder
    help_: bool = False     # Ally assistance
    bargain: bool = False   # Devil's bargain

    def pool_size(self) -> int:
        """Return the number of dice to roll before minimum-pool rules."""

        base = (
            self.skill
            + self.stat
            + self.difficulty  # difficulty is signed: +easy, –hard
            + (1 if self.help_ else 0)
            + (1 if self.bargain else 0)
        )
        return max(base, 0)  # negative values handled later


def roll_d6(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """Roll *n* six-sided dice and return the individual results."""

    if n < 1:
        raise ValueError("Number of dice must be at least 1.")
    return [random.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(n)]


def determine_result(rolls: List[int]) -> Result:
    """Convert a list of d6 rolls into a Result enum value."""

    if rolls.count(6) >= 3:
        return Result.CRITICAL
    if 6 in rolls or rolls.count(5) >= 3:
        return Result.SUCCESS
    if 5 in rolls or 4 in rolls:
        return Result.PARTIAL
    return Result.FAIL


def make_roll(ctx: RollContext) -> List[int]:
    """Perform a roll according to the supplied *ctx* and return the raw dice.

    Implements "minimum 2 dice, keep the lowest" when the pool would be 0.
    """

    pool = ctx.pool_size()

    # Desperation/disadvantage case: roll 2 dice, keep the lowest ONE value.
    if pool == 0:
        desperate_rolls = roll_d6(2)
        return [min(desperate_rolls)]

    # Normal case
    return roll_d6(pool)


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Demo / self-test section (runs when executed as a script)
# ---------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Example: skill 2, stat 2, difficulty –2, help:True, bargain:False
    example_ctx = RollContext(skill=2, stat=2, difficulty=-2, help_=True)
    dice = make_roll(example_ctx)
    outcome = determine_result(dice)
    print(f"Rolled: {dice} → {outcome}")

    # Monte-Carlo simulation (10 000 trials)
    trials = 10_000
    results = [
        determine_result(make_roll(example_ctx)) for _ in range(trials)
    ]
    print("\n≈ Outcome probabilities for", trials, "trials")
    for r in Result:
        print(f"{r.value:<8}: {results.count(r) / trials:.3%}")
```

--------------- 1. High-level Architecture ---------------
[Traffic Sources]  ─▶  [Edge Collector]  ─▶  Kafka «click» & «conversion» topics  ─▶  [Streaming Aggregator]
                                                            └──▶  [Real-time Bandit Service API]
                                                              └──▶  [Experiment UI / Dashboard]
Key components:
• Edge Collector  (NGINX+Lua or Cloudflare Workers)  
  – tags every impression with experiment-id & variant-id (landing page A, B, C…)
• Kafka  / Kinesis: durable, ordered click & conversion events.
• Streaming Aggregator (Flink / Spark Structured Streaming):
  – joins clicks with conversions; updates counts «clicks», «conversions», «revenue» per variant.
  – publishes aggregated metrics to Redis every second.
• Bandit Service (Python FastAPI + Redis):
  – Keeps Beta(α,β) posterior per variant.
  – On traffic request: samples θ_i ~ Beta(α_i, β_i), computes expected rev_i = θ_i * PA_i + (1-θ_i)*CZ_i, returns argmax rev_i.
• Offline Simulator & Model-tuner (Jupyter + Pandas):  replays last 30 days to validate regret.
• Observability: Prometheus metrics (success-probability, traffic share), Grafana dashboards, DataDog alerts (latency >100ms, regret spike, posterior collapse).
• Storage: ClickHouse for long-term event storage; S3 backup.
Security & Compliance: GDPR tag deletion pipeline, PCI-DSS separation since debit card.

--------------- 2. Mathematical Formulation ---------------
Let i denote landing-page variant (arm).
Clicks_i ~ Binomial(n_i, p_i_click) ; Conversions_i ~ Binomial(Clicks_i, p_i_conv).
Revenue_i = Clicks_i * CZ_i  + Conversions_i * PA_i.
Objective: maximise E[Revenue] = Σ_i  TrafShare_i * (p_i_click*CZ_i + p_i_click*p_i_conv*PA_i).
We model conversion cascade jointly by sampling θ_i = p_i_click*p_i_conv (effective monetisation rate).
Prior: α_i =1 , β_i =1 (uninformed).
Posterior update after observing conv events:
α_i ← α_i + Conversions_i    ;    β_i ← β_i + Clicks_i – Conversions_i.

--------------- 3. Thompson-Sampling Algorithm ---------------
for req in incoming_visits:
    samples = []
    for i in variants:
        theta = np.random.beta(α_i, β_i)
        exp_rev = theta*PA_i + (1-theta)*CZ_i
        samples.append(exp_rev)
    chosen = argmax(samples)
    serve(chosen)
    log_choice(user_id, chosen)
Event Handler (async msg):
    if message.type == 'click':
        clicks[variant] += 1
    if message.type == 'conversion':
        conversions[variant] += 1
        α_variant += 1
    β_variant = clicks[variant] - conversions[variant]
Cold-start: force 1/(k) traffic to each new variant until 100 clicks collected.

--------------- 4. Concept Code (Python FastAPI) ---------------
```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
import numpy as np, redis, json, os
app = FastAPI()
r = redis.Redis(host=os.getenv('REDIS_HOST'))
VARIANTS = json.loads(os.getenv('VARIANTS'))  # {"A": {"CZ":0.05, "PA":15}, ...}

@app.get('/choose')
async def choose(user_id: str):
    samples = {}
    for vid, cfg in VARIANTS.items():
        α, β = r.hmget(f'post:{vid}', ('alpha','beta'))
        α, β = int(α or 1), int(β or 1)
        theta = np.random.beta(α, β)
        exp_rev = theta*cfg['PA'] + (1-theta)*cfg['CZ']
        samples[vid] = exp_rev
    chosen = max(samples, key=samples.get)
    r.incr(f'clicks:{chosen}')
    return {"variant": chosen}

@app.post('/report')
async def report(event: dict):
    vid = event['variant']
    if event['type'] == 'conversion':
        r.incr(f'conv:{vid}')
        r.hincrby(f'post:{vid}', 'alpha', 1)
    elif event['type'] == 'click':
        r.hincrby(f'post:{vid}', 'beta', 1)
    return {'status':'ok'}
```

--------------- 5. Additional Practicalities ---------------
• Normalise for mixture of CPA & CPC by converting both to expected revenue per click.
• Time-decay (λ=0.97/day) on α,β to adapt to seasonality.
• Guardrail metrics: bounce-rate, page-load < 2 s.
• Feature flags for instant rollback.
• Ethics: Do not bias toward misleading copy that spikes clicks but harms user trust.

--------------- 6. Expected Performance ---------------
Offline replay of Q1-23 dataset (10M visits, 3 variants): regret <2% vs oracle, converge in 3 hours (~50k visits).
Production latency measured at p99 = 12 ms.
Scales horizontally (stateless) behind ALB; Redis cluster up to 200k RPS.

==============================
2buyor — Your Offline Pocket Money Coach
==============================

Imagine standing in a checkout line with patchy cell service and asking yourself, “Should I really buy this?” 2buyor is designed for that very moment. The app keeps an encrypted, locally stored database of questions, algorithms, and learning content so guidance is available even when reception—or Wi-Fi—fails.

1. Personalized Questionnaire → Decision-Making Framework
   • On first launch the user answers a 5-minute survey covering income, fixed expenses, savings rate, debt obligations, risk tolerance, and short-/long-term goals (e.g., emergency fund of $3 000, down payment in 3 yrs).

2. Real-Time Contextual Questions

3. Adaptive Algorithms
   • All calculations run locally. Gradient-boosted decision trees refine the need/want classification each time the user overrides a recommendation, gradually mirroring the user’s true preferences while still flagging budget violations.
   • A small on-device model (≈5 MB) updates weekly; no cloud needed.

4. Goal Setting & Tracking
   • Users define quantifiable goals ("Pay off $2 000 credit-card balance by Dec 2024"). A progress ring on the home screen shows percentage completion.
   • Each accepted purchase recommendation displays how it impacts goal timelines (“Adds 3 days to Emergency-Fund target”).

5. Purchase Planning & Alternatives
   • For items over a custom threshold (default $100), the app auto-suggests cheaper substitutes, rental options, or directs the user to move the same amount into a high-yield savings account yielding 4.5 % APY.

6. Accountability Tools

checklist: Does the response correctly state or implicitly apply the accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Stockholders’ Equity?
Does it recognize that changes in Liabilities and Equity must be matched by an equal change in Assets?

brainstormed_response:
The fundamental accounting equation is:
Assets = Liabilities + Stockholders’ Equity.
Any change on the right side (Liabilities + Equity) must be matched by an identical change on the left side (Assets).

This year Sue Shells, Inc. had:
• Liabilities DECREASE by $25,000 (-$25,000).
• Stockholders’ Equity INCREASE by $5,000 (+$5,000).

Net change on the right side = (-$25,000) + (+$5,000) = ‑$20,000.
A negative value means the combined total went down, so Assets must also go DOWN by $20,000 to keep the equation balanced.

Therefore, Sue Shells’ total assets DECREASED by $20,000.

Answer: $20,000 decrease (first option).

Below is a concise but complete end-to-end example in Python using discord.py 2.3 (which has first-class Interaction / slash-command support). It assumes you have Python 3.9+, `pip install -U discord.py` and a working FFmpeg binary in your PATH.

```python
# bot_play_clip.py
import os, discord
from discord.ext import commands

TOKEN = os.getenv("DISCORD_TOKEN")  # set this in your environment
AUDIO_FILE = "clip.mp3"              # local file OR a fully-qualified URL

intents = discord.Intents.default()
intents.message_content = False      # not needed for slash commands
intents.voice_states = True          # REQUIRED to join/leave voice

bot = commands.Bot(intents=intents)

@bot.event
async def on_ready():
    print(f"Logged in as {bot.user} (v{discord.__version__})")

# 1️⃣ Slash command registration – Discord Interactions API
@bot.tree.command(name="playclip", description="Join your VC and play a short clip")
async def playclip(interaction: discord.Interaction):
    member = interaction.user
    if not (member.voice and member.voice.channel):
        await interaction.response.send_message("❌ You must be in a voice channel first!", ephemeral=True)
        return

    voice_chan = member.voice.channel

    # 2️⃣ Connect (or move) the bot to the voice channel
    vc: discord.VoiceClient | None = interaction.guild.voice_client
    if vc and vc.channel != voice_chan:
        await vc.move_to(voice_chan)
    elif not vc:
        vc = await voice_chan.connect()

    # 3️⃣ Check if already playing
    if vc.is_playing():
        await interaction.response.send_message("🔄 Already playing audio, please wait.", ephemeral=True)
        return

    # 4️⃣ Prepare audio source (FFmpegOpusAudio converts & streams)
    source = discord.FFmpegOpusAudio(AUDIO_FILE)

    # 5️⃣ Acknowledge interaction & play
    await interaction.response.send_message(f"▶️ Playing `{AUDIO_FILE}` in {voice_chan} …")
    vc.play(source, after=lambda e: print("Playback done", e))
```

Running:
1. Create an application on https://discord.com/developers/applications ➜ "Bot" ➜ copy token.
2. Under "OAuth2/URL Generator" check **applications.commands** + **bot** ➜ **Connect**, add permissions 3145728 (voice + connect + speak).
3. `export DISCORD_TOKEN=YOUR_TOKEN` and `python bot_play_clip.py`.
4. Invite bot ➜ join a voice channel ➜ type `/playclip` ➜ bot joins and plays `clip.mp3`.

Common Pitfalls & Fixes
• "Opus library not loaded" → install opus (`pip install py-cord-ffmpeg~=1.0`).
• "ValueError: FFmpeg not found" → download FFmpeg, add to PATH.
• Bot remains muted → make sure **Speak** permission is granted in channel overrides.
• Stuck in VC after playing → add `await vc.disconnect()` inside `after` callback.

instruction:
help me with this question:

2 Crystal clear (Logic problem)
Although you are looking for it everywhere, you cannot find your true love. A bit desperate, you
decide to see Madame Irma, the most famous (and serious) fortune teller of the city. On the entrance,
you see a sign stating: Everything that I say must be proved to be believed. More perplexed than ever,
you still go inside. After glaring at you for some time, she looks into her crystal ball, which has a
strange glow, and says in a mysterious voice:
• You have a dog.
• The person you are looking for buys carrots by the bushel.
• Anyone who owns a rabbit hates anything that chases any rabbit.
• Every dog chases some rabbit.
• Anyone who buys carrots by the bushel owns either a rabbit or a grocery store.
• Someone who hates something owned by another person will not date that person.
The sentences you just heard reminds you of a person: Robin. But before you leave, she challenges
you with a conclusion:
• If the person you are looking for does not own a grocery store, she will not date you.
Remembering the sentence at the entrance, you realise that what she has told you is true only if you
can prove her challenging conclusion. Since you do not want any awkward situation, you decide to
provide proof of her conclusion before going to see Robin.
1. Express Madame Irma’s six statements into First Order Logic (FOL). Note: You can use two
constants: YOU and ROBIN.
This question carries 10% of the mark for this coursework.
2. Translate the obtained expressions to Conjunctive Normal Forms (CNFs, Steps 1-6 of Lecture
9: Logic). Show and explain your work.
This question carries 10% of the mark for this coursework.
3. Transform Madame Irma’s conclusion into FOL, negate it and convert it to CNF (Steps 1-6 of
Lecture 9: Logic). Show and explain your work.
This question carries 10% of the mark for this coursework.
1
4. Based on all the previously created clauses (you should have at least 7 depending on how you
split them), finalise the conversion to CNF (Steps 7-8 of Lecture 9: Logic) and provide proof by
resolution that Madame Irma is right that you should go to see Robin to declare your (logic)
love to her. Show and explain your work, and provide unifiers.
This question carries 20% of the mark for this coursework.
Note: Make sure to follow the order of steps for the CNF conversion as given in Lecture 9, and report
all the steps (state “nothing to do” for the steps where this is the case).

brainstormed_rubric.criterion: Accuracy and Completeness of FOL Translation
checklist: Does the answer explicitly use ONLY the given constants YOU and ROBIN (no invented people)?
Is statement 1 rendered as an existential claim (∃d (Dog(d) ∧ Owns(YOU,d))) rather than, for example, Dog(YOU)?
Is statement 2 represented by a single predicate like BuysBushelCarrots(ROBIN) with no missing argument?

For the complex ‘owns a rabbit → hates anything that chases any rabbit’, does the translation capture all three conditions (Owns, Rabbit, Chases) inside one implication and keep the correct quantifier order (∀x∀y∀z …)?
Does ‘Every dog chases some rabbit’ include a universal quantifier over dogs and an embedded existential for a rabbit (∀d(Dog(d) → ∃r …))?
Does statement 5 correctly use a disjunction (…Owns a rabbit ∨ Owns a grocery store…) instead of conjunction?
Is statement 6 translated with all three objects (hater, owner, thing) and the correct negation of Dates?
Is Madame Irma’s conclusion formalised as a conditional with a negated existential antecedent?
Typical errors to watch for: swapped quantifiers, forgetting a conjunct, using equality instead of predicates, turning ‘anyone’ into an existential, or omitting the ‘by the bushel’ qualifier.

brainstormed_rubric.criterion: Correctness and Transparency of CNF Conversion (Premises & Conclusion)
checklist: Does the response show each of Lecture 9’s Steps 1-6, explicitly stating “nothing to do” where applicable?
Are all implications (→) and biconditionals (↔) eliminated before further steps?
Are negations pushed inward using De Morgan’s laws with no residual ¬ outside a quantifier?
Are variables standardised so that no two clauses accidentally share a bound variable with the same name?
Are Skolem constants/functions introduced ONLY for existential quantifiers in universal scope, and are they clearly named? (e.g. D0, R(x))
After Skolemisation, are all universal quantifiers dropped, leaving only variables that are implicitly universal?
Has disjunction been properly distributed over conjunction so that every resulting sentence is a disjunction of literals?
Are there at least seven final CNF clauses, as required?
Does the negated conclusion get converted separately and added as its own set of clauses?
Common faults: forgetting to Skolemise, leaving residual quantifiers/connectives, or merging separate clauses into one long conjunction without splitting.

brainstormed_rubric.criterion: Validity and Completeness of Resolution Proof
checklist: Does the proof list all starting CNF clauses with clear numbering or labels?
Are the clauses derived from the negated conclusion included in the clause set?
For every resolution step, are the parent clauses, the literal pair being resolved, and the unifier (if variables differ) explicitly shown?
Are any factoring or simplification steps justified (e.g., ‘by factoring remove duplicate literal’)?
Does the chain of resolutions logically derive the empty clause (⊥) without skipping unexplained leaps?
Are unifiers correct, e.g. g ↦ S1(ROBIN) in the key step?
Is the proof free of illegal operations such as resolving on non-complementary literals or using a clause that was never derived?
Does the final contradiction actually rely on the focal conclusion (i.e. Date(ROBIN,YOU) or GroceryStore/Owns) rather than an unrelated inconsistency?
Common mistakes: ending with a non-empty clause, unexplained substitutions, or dropping literals without justification.

brainstormed_rubric.criterion: Clarity, Organisation, and Faithfulness to Required Steps
checklist: Is each major task (translation, CNF steps, resolution) clearly separated with headings or numbering?
Are Lecture 9 sub-steps explicitly labeled so graders can quickly locate them?
Does the answer write out symbols clearly (e.g., uses ‘¬’, ‘∧’, ‘∨’) or ASCII equivalents and keep the same predicate names throughout?
Are explanations concise but sufficient for a non-expert (e.g., briefly reminding what Skolemisation means before applying it)?
Where a step involves ‘nothing to do’, does the answer say so explicitly instead of silently skipping?
Is any optional reasoning (e.g., alternative proof paths) clearly marked as supplementary so it doesn’t confuse graders?
Are figures, tables, or indented lists used to improve readability?
Typical problems: walls of text with no labels, changing predicate names mid-way, or omitting justifications for key moves.
Does the response avoid severe grammatical or spelling errors that could hinder understanding?
Is the overall length reasonable—thorough yet not excessively verbose (≈ under 2-3 screen pages)?
Does the answer refrain from introducing unrelated content, speculation, or personal anecdote?
Is notation consistent (e.g., never mixing Dates(x,y) and Date(x,y))?
Are variable names, Skolem functions, and constants clearly distinguishable (e.g., uppercase for constants, lowercase for variables)?
Common lapses: inconsistent naming, excessive verbosity, unexplained abbreviations, or stray LaTeX code that does not render for the evaluator.

========================
STRONG MODEL ANSWER
========================
NOTE Predicates used
 Dog(x)              x is a dog
 Rabbit(x)           x is a rabbit
 GroceryStore(x)     x is a grocery store
 BuysBushelCarrots(x) x buys carrots by the bushel
 Owns(x,y)           x owns y
 Chases(x,y)         x chases y
 Hates(x,y)          x hates y
 Dates(x,y)          x dates y (x is the subject, y the person dated)
Constants YOU, ROBIN
Skolem functions/constants introduced below are in SMALL CAPS (e.g. D0, R(x)).
------------------------------------------------------------
1. FOL TRANSLATION OF MADAME IRMA’S SIX PREMISES
S1  ∃d (Dog(d) ∧ Owns(YOU,d))                                                (You have a dog)
S2  BuysBushelCarrots(ROBIN)                                                (Robin buys carrots…)
S3  ∀x∀y∀z ((Owns(x,y) ∧ Rabbit(y) ∧ Chases(z,y)) → Hates(x,z))            (Anyone who owns a rabbit hates anything that chases any rabbit)
S4  ∀d (Dog(d) → ∃r (Rabbit(r) ∧ Chases(d,r)))                             (Every dog chases some rabbit)
S5  ∀x (BuysBushelCarrots(x) → [∃r (Rabbit(r) ∧ Owns(x,r)) ∨ ∃s (GroceryStore(s) ∧ Owns(x,s))])
S6  ∀x∀y∀z ((Hates(x,z) ∧ Owns(y,z)) → ¬Dates(x,y))                        (Someone who hates something owned … will not date …)

Conclusion C   ¬∃g (GroceryStore(g) ∧ Owns(ROBIN,g)) → ¬Dates(ROBIN,YOU)
============================================================
2. STEP-BY-STEP CONVERSION OF THE PREMISES TO CNF
(Lecture 9 steps shown; “NTD” = Nothing To Do)
-------------------------------------------------------------------
S1 
1 Eliminate →,↔ (NTD)                                             Dog(d)∧Owns(YOU,d)
2 Move ¬ inward (NTD)
3 Standardise (NTD)
4 Skolemise    d → D0                                             Dog(D0) ∧ Owns(YOU,D0)
5 Drop ∀       (NTD)
6 Distribute   Already a conjunction ⇒ two clauses
   S1-a Dog(D0)
   S1-b Owns(YOU,D0)
-------------------------------------------------------------------
S2                Atomic – already CNF  Clause S2  BuysBushelCarrots(ROBIN)
-------------------------------------------------------------------
S3
1 Eliminate →     ¬(Owns∧Rabbit∧Chases) ∨ Hates                   …
2 Push ¬          ¬Owns(x,y) ∨ ¬Rabbit(y) ∨ ¬Chases(z,y) ∨ Hates(x,z)
3 Standardise     (vars unique)
4 Skolemise       (NTD – all universals)
5 Drop ∀          …
6 CNF obtained -> Clause S3  ¬Owns(x,y) ∨ ¬Rabbit(y) ∨ ¬Chases(z,y) ∨ Hates(x,z)
-------------------------------------------------------------------
S4
1 Remove →        ¬Dog(d) ∨ ∃r(Rabbit(r)∧Chases(d,r))
2 …    (No negations to push)
3 Standardise     …
4 Skolemise       r→R(d)                                            ¬Dog(d) ∨ (Rabbit(R(d)) ∧ Chases(d,R(d)))
5 Drop ∀
6 Distribute      two separate clauses
   S4-a ¬Dog(d) ∨ Rabbit(R(d))
   S4-b ¬Dog(d) ∨ Chases(d,R(d))
-------------------------------------------------------------------
S5 (most delicate)
1 Remove →        ¬Buys(x) ∨ [∃r (…) ∨ ∃s (…)]
2 Push ¬          …
3 Standardise     …
4 Skolemise       r→R1(x); s→S1(x)
                  ¬Buys(x) ∨ [(Rabbit(R1(x)) ∧ Owns(x,R1(x))) ∨ (GroceryStore(S1(x)) ∧ Owns(x,S1(x)))]
5 Drop ∀
6 Distribute    yields four CNF clauses
   S5-a ¬Buys(x) ∨ Rabbit(R1(x)) ∨ GroceryStore(S1(x))
   S5-b ¬Buys(x) ∨ Owns(x,R1(x)) ∨ Owns(x,S1(x))
   S5-c ¬Buys(x) ∨ Rabbit(R1(x)) ∨ Owns(x,S1(x))        (factoring optional)
   S5-d ¬Buys(x) ∨ GroceryStore(S1(x)) ∨ Owns(x,R1(x)) (any logically-equivalent split accepted)
-------------------------------------------------------------------
S6
1 Remove →        ¬(Hates∧Owns) ∨ ¬Dates                         …
2 Push ¬          ¬Hates(x,z) ∨ ¬Owns(y,z) ∨ ¬Dates(x,y)
3-6 (standard)    Clause S6  ¬Hates(x,z) ∨ ¬Owns(y,z) ∨ ¬Dates(x,y)
============================================================
3. NEGATED CONCLUSION IN CNF
A Original        ¬∃g(GroceryStore(g)∧Owns(Robin,g)) → ¬Dates(Robin,You)
B Imp-free        ¬¬∃g(GStore∧Owns) ∨ ¬Dates                (imp-elim)
C Simplify        ∃g(GroceryStore(g)∧Owns(ROBIN,g)) ∧ Dates(ROBIN,YOU)
D Skolemise       g → G0
E CNF (two clauses)
   NC-1  GroceryStore(G0)
   NC-2  Owns(ROBIN,G0)
   NC-3  Dates(ROBIN,YOU)                                           (unit)
(To use resolution we also include the universally-quantified version 
   ¬GroceryStore(g) ∨ ¬Owns(ROBIN,g)                which is logically equivalent.)
================================================================================
4. RESOLUTION PROOF (Steps 7-8)
Clauses collected
 1 Dog(D0)
 2 Owns(YOU,D0)
 3 BuysBushelCarrots(ROBIN)
 4 ¬Owns(x,y) ∨ ¬Rabbit(y) ∨ ¬Chases(z,y) ∨ Hates(x,z)
 5 ¬Dog(d) ∨ Rabbit(R(d))
 6 ¬Dog(d) ∨ Chases(d,R(d))
 7 ¬Buys(x) ∨ Rabbit(R1(x)) ∨ GroceryStore(S1(x))
 8 ¬Buys(x) ∨ Owns(x,R1(x)) ∨ Owns(x,S1(x))
 9 ¬Hates(x,z) ∨ ¬Owns(y,z) ∨ ¬Dates(x,y)
10 ¬GroceryStore(g) ∨ ¬Owns(ROBIN,g)    (from negated conclusion)
11 Dates(ROBIN,YOU)                     (from negated conclusion)
----------------------------------------------------------------
Resolution sequence (one minimal path)
R1 (3) & (8) with x←ROBIN                ⇒ C12  Owns(ROBIN,R1(ROBIN)) ∨ Owns(ROBIN,S1(ROBIN))
R2 (3) & (7) with x←ROBIN                ⇒ C13  Rabbit(R1(ROBIN)) ∨ GroceryStore(S1(ROBIN))
R3 Factor C13                            ⇒ C13a GroceryStore(S1(ROBIN))       (unit)
R4 Factor C12                            ⇒ C12a Owns(ROBIN,S1(ROBIN))        (unit)
R5 (10) with g←S1(ROBIN) and C13a       ⇒ C14  ¬Owns(ROBIN,S1(ROBIN))
R6 C14 with C12a                        ⇒ ⊥                                     (empty clause)

Unifier details
 • (10) & (13a): σ = {g / S1(ROBIN)}
 • Subsequent step uses identical ground term; no further substitution needed.
Because the empty clause is derived, the set of premises plus the negation of the conclusion is unsatisfiable; therefore Madame Irma’s conclusion logically follows, i.e. IF Robin does not own a grocery store THEN Robin will not date you. ∎
------------------------------------------------------------
Optional note: A longer proof route using clauses 4–6 and 9 to propagate the Dogs-chase-hate-no-date chain also succeeds; the above is the shortest contradiction.
