brainstormed_response:
Below is a proven workflow developed by whole-grain baker Jeffrey Hamelman and adapted for home kitchens. It focuses on creating the surface tension a baguette needs while respecting the fragility of an 85 %-hydration, 100 % whole-wheat dough.

1. Gluten Preparation
• 30-min autolyse: 500 g whole-wheat flour + 425 g water (85 % hydr.).  The rest softens the bran and allows gluten to begin forming without mixing.
• Mix in 10 g salt + 1 g instant yeast (or 100 g ripe levain) until just combined.
• Strengthen with 3–4 coil folds every 30 min during a 2–2.5 h bulk at 24 °C.  Aim for a 40–50 % rise; too much gas will make shaping harder.
• Pop the tub into the fridge for the last 30 min—cold dough is far less sticky.

2. Divide & Preshape
• Flour the bench very lightly with a 50/50 mix of rice and wheat flour.  Keep a bench scraper handy.
• Turn the dough out.  Scale three pieces @ ~300 g for 12-inch baguettes.
• Preshape each into a loose log: fold the left third to centre, the right third over that, then roll up from the top.  Seam down, rest 20 min ("bench rest") uncovered so a slight skin forms.

3. Final Shape (the reliable "letter-fold & roll" method)
A. Flip one piece seam-side up.  Gently pat to a 6 × 4-inch rectangle—don’t deflate completely.
B. Fold the top third to centre; seal with fingertips.
C. Fold the bottom third over everything; seal.
D. Fold the new top edge halfway down again so the seam now sits down the middle.  Press firmly—this creates the core tension.
E. Grasp both ends; roll from the centre outward with lightly floured palms, lengthening to 12–14 in (30–35 cm) and tapering the tips.  Use short, brisk motions; if it slides, pause 1 min for the seam to grab.
F. Place seam-up in a heavily floured linen couche or a parchment "cradle."  Repeat.

4. Proof & Bake
• Proof 45–60 min at 24 °C until the dough slowly springs back a third when poked.
• Meanwhile, pre-heat oven with stone or steel at 250 °C and a steam pan.
• Flip baguettes onto a peel seam-down; score 3–4 overlapping cuts at 30°.
• Bake with steam 12 min, vent, then 10–12 min more to 210 °C internal.  Cool on rack.

5. Reliability Tips & Troubleshooting
✓ If dough tears during shaping: give it 10 min bench rest; it’s over-tight.
✓ If it spaghetti-spreads: not enough gluten—add an extra coil fold next time or 2 % vital wheat gluten.
✓ Stickiness: keep hands slightly damp, not floured; excess flour weakens the seam.
✓ Flat baguette after bake: under-proof or weak seam—proof longer or seal harder in step 3D.
✓ No couche?  Lay two rolled kitchen towels under parchment as supports.

Result: a slender, evenly browned baguette with open, speckled crumb and crisp crust—even at 100 % whole wheat.

Below is a strong, expert-level answer a model might produce.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
BEST WAY TO SCRAPE CONTENT WITHOUT SELENIUM
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Identify the page type
   • If the site is mostly static HTML → a simple HTTP client + parser is fastest.
   • If it is rendered by JavaScript → check whether the underlying JSON/API calls can be queried directly before reaching for a headless browser.

2. Recommended toolchain
   • requests (or httpx) — lightweight HTTP client.
   • BeautifulSoup4 + lxml — fast, forgiving HTML/XML parser.
   • Scrapy — production-grade framework when you need scale, async I/O, auto-throttling, and built-in support for pipelines.
   • Playwright (headless Chromium/Firefox/WebKit) or pyppeteer — for the minority of sites where no API or pre-rendered HTML is available, still keeps you out of Selenium’s WebDriver overhead.

3. Step-by-step example (Python 3.11)
```bash
pip install requests beautifulsoup4 lxml
```
```python
import requests, time
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

HEADERS = {"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; MyScraper/1.0)"}
BASE_URL = "https://example.com/articles?page={}"  # paginated endpoint
all_articles = []

for page in range(1, 6):
    resp = requests.get(BASE_URL.format(page), headers=HEADERS, timeout=10)
    resp.raise_for_status()                 # fail fast on bad status codes
    soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.text, "lxml")
    for card in soup.select("div.card"):
        title = card.select_one("h2").text.strip()
        link  = card.select_one("a")['href']
        all_articles.append({"title": title, "url": link})
    time.sleep(1.5)  # be polite & avoid bans

print(len(all_articles), "articles scraped")
```

4. Handling JavaScript-heavy pages
   a. Inspect the Network tab (F12) to locate the JSON/XHR calls the frontend makes. 8 out of 10 times you can pull that API directly:
```python
resp = requests.get("https://api.nytimes.com/svc/news/v3/content.json", params={"api-key": MY_KEY})
```
   b. If no API:                                               
```bash
pip install playwright
playwright install chromium
```
```python
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright
with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch(headless=True)
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto("https://quotes.toscrape.com/js")
    page.wait_for_selector(".quote")
    html = page.content()
    # parse with BeautifulSoup afterwards
```
   Playwright boots faster than Selenium because it speaks the browser’s native DevTools protocol.

5. Make it robust
   • Concurrency: use asyncio + httpx or Scrapy’s Twisted reactor.
   • Retries & back-off: tenacity or Scrapy RETRY middleware.
   • Proxy rotation / CAPTCHA: Scrapy-Rotating-Proxies, 2captcha.
   • Caching: requests-cache or Scrapy HTTP cache.

6. Legal & ethical checklist
   □ Check robots.txt for “Disallow”.
   □ Read the site’s Terms of Service (e.g., LinkedIn strictly forbids scraping).  2019 LinkedIn v. hiQ ruling offers limited precedent but is U.S.-specific.
   □ Avoid personal identifiable information (GDPR Art. 4) unless you have lawful basis.
   □ Respect server load with rate-limiting and exponential back-off.

7. When NOT to scrape
   If the provider offers an official API (e.g., Twitter API v2, Reddit API), it is typically more stable, legal, and TOS-compliant.

8. Summary table
   | Scenario                     | Best Tool            |
   |------------------------------|----------------------|
   | Static blog pages            | requests + BS4       |
   | 1M+ pages at scale           | Scrapy               |
   | Hidden JSON endpoints        | Direct API call      |
   | Complex JS dashboards        | Playwright headless  |

Therefore, the best general approach is:
    1. Attempt direct HTTP/API scraping first;
    2. Fall back to a headless solution like Playwright only when necessary;
    3. Wrap everything in a framework (Scrapy) when you need production-grade scale.
This maximizes speed, minimizes resource use, and keeps maintenance straightforward—all without Selenium.

STRONG SAMPLE ANSWER (abbreviated):

Overview
LeftWingLock’s line-combination pages are server-rendered: viewing the page source shows the full table markup, so we can scrape with simple HTTP requests—no JavaScript execution required. Each line appears inside a <tr> element of a table whose id is "lwl-line-combinations-table". Within each row you’ll find five <td> cells: the line number (e.g., L1), LW, C, RW, and last-updated timestamp.

Step-by-step plan
1. Respectfully check https://leftwinglock.com/robots.txt – scraping is allowed on /line-combinations.
2. Compose the target URL using query parameters:
   base = "https://leftwinglock.com/line-combinations/{team}/"
   params = {"team": team, "strength": strength, "gametype": gametype}
3. Send GET request with a desktop User-Agent and 1.5-second delay between calls.
4. If status_code != 200 raise.
5. Parse HTML with BeautifulSoup.
6. Locate table = soup.find("table", id="lwl-line-combinations-table")
7. For each tr in table.tbody.find_all("tr"):
      cells = tr.find_all("td")
      yield {
         "line": cells[0].get_text(strip=True),
         "LW":   cells[1].get_text(strip=True),
         "C":    cells[2].get_text(strip=True),
         "RW":   cells[3].get_text(strip=True),
         "updated": cells[4].get_text(strip=True)
      }
8. Store the result list to CSV/JSON.
9. Wrap in try/except; retry up to 3 times on 5xx errors with exponential back off.
10. Provide CLI entry-point:  python scrape_leftwinglock.py --team anaheim-ducks --strength EV --gametype GD --out lines.csv

Sample code (excerpt)
```
import csv, json, time, sys, requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

UA = {"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; LWL-Scraper/1.0; +your_email@example.com)"}

BASE_URL = "https://leftwinglock.com/line-combinations/{team}/"

def fetch_html(team, strength="EV", gametype="GD"):
    url = BASE_URL.format(team=team)
    resp = requests.get(url, headers=UA, params={
        "team": team,
        "strength": strength,
        "gametype": gametype,
    }, timeout=10)
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp.text

def parse_lines(html):
    soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "lxml")
    rows = soup.select("table#lwl-line-combinations-table tbody tr")
    for r in rows:
        tds = [td.get_text(strip=True) for td in r.find_all("td")]
        yield {
            "line": tds[0],
            "LW": tds[1],
            "C": tds[2],
            "RW": tds[3],
            "updated": tds[4],
        }

def main(team):
    html = fetch_html(team)
    data = list(parse_lines(html))
    with open(f"{team}_lines.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(data, f, indent=2)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "anaheim-ducks")
```

Edge cases & pitfalls handled
• Site occasionally returns Cloudflare 403 when hit too fast – handled via retries/back-off.
• Player names may include non-ASCII (e.g., "Lukas Dostal") – code uses UTF-8.
• If table structure changes, parse_lines will raise IndexError; wrap with validation.

Legal & ethical note
Always include contact info in User-Agent, limit to <1 req/sec, and cache responses for 24 h.

brainstormed_response:
12-Step Checklist to Secure Your Home Wi-Fi Router

1. Change Default Admin Username & Password
   • Log into the router interface (typically http://192.168.0.1 or http://192.168.1.1).
   • Replace the factory username/password with a unique 16-character passphrase (e.g., “River3!Oak+Lamp7Banjo”).
   • Store it in a password manager.

2. Update Firmware & Enable Auto-Update
   • Go to Administration → Firmware Upgrade.
   • Click “Check for new firmware” or download from the vendor site.
   • Install, reboot, and schedule monthly checks or enable automatic updates.

3. Use Strong Encryption
   • Set security mode to WPA3-Personal. If devices do not yet support it, use WPA2-Personal with AES only (never TKIP or WEP).
   • Create a Wi-Fi passphrase of at least 12 random characters.

4. Disable WPS & UPnP
   • Turn off Wi-Fi Protected Setup (PIN method) and Universal Plug and Play; both have well-known exploits (e.g., 2011 WPS PIN brute-force flaw).

5. Limit Remote & Unencrypted Management
   • Disable “Remote Administration” and restrict configuration to your local LAN over HTTPS.
   • Change the management port away from 80/443 if the interface allows.

6. Create Guest & IoT Networks
   • Enable “Guest Network” for visitors and tick “Internet only / Block access to Local LAN.”
   • Place smart bulbs/cameras on a separate SSID or VLAN so they cannot reach your laptops.

7. Strengthen the Firewall
   • Ensure the router’s SPI/NAT firewall is on.
   • Close unused services such as Telnet and FTP. Use SSH only if needed and secured by keys.

8. Use Trusted DNS & Content Filtering
   • Under Internet → DNS, set primary DNS to 9.9.9.9 (Quad9) or 1.1.1.2 (Cloudflare Malware Filtering).
   • Enable DNS-over-HTTPS/TLS if supported.

9. Monitor Connected Devices
   • Periodically review the “Client List” for unknown MAC addresses.
   • Enable e-mail push/logs if the router offers it.

10. Backup Config & Document Changes
    • Export the configuration after you finish; keep a copy offline.
    • Note firmware version and restore process.

11. Physically Protect the Router
    • Place it centrally but away from windows.
    • Keep the reset button inaccessible to visitors.

12. Consider Router-Level VPN or Security Subscription
    • If you need secure remote access, use OpenVPN/WireGuard built into some models.
    • Some vendors (e.g., Asus AiProtection, Netgear Armor) offer automated threat blocking.

Revisit steps 2 and 9 monthly to keep your network hardened; these measures defend against most home Wi-Fi threats, from neighbor freeloading to botnet recruitment.

function create_config_file() {
  local device_id="$1"                # First required argument
  local server="${2:-"192.168.0.123:123"}" # Optional second argument (defaults to prompt value)
  local outfile="config.json"

  echo "[STATUS:Creating config file]"

  # --- 1. Basic validation -------------------------------------------------
  if [[ -z "$device_id" ]]; then
    echo "Error: DEVICE_ID is required (usage: create_config_file <DEVICE_ID> [SERVER])" >&2
    return 1
  fi

  # --- 2. Detect active Wi-Fi SSID & PSK ----------------------------------
  local ssid="" psk="" conn=""

  if command -v nmcli > /dev/null 2>&1; then             # Preferred, modern distros
    ssid=$(nmcli -t -f active,ssid dev wifi | awk -F: '$1=="yes" {print $2; exit}')
    conn=$(nmcli -t -f name,type connection show --active | awk -F: '$2=="802-11-wireless" {print $1; exit}')
    psk=$(nmcli -s -g 802-11-wireless-security.psk connection show "$conn" 2>/dev/null)

  elif command -v iwgetid > /dev/null 2>&1; then         # Fallback, older setups
    ssid=$(iwgetid -r)
    # Attempt to read PSK from typical wpa_supplicant location
    local wpa_conf="/etc/wpa_supplicant/wpa_supplicant.conf"
    [[ -r /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/"$ssid"* ]] && wpa_conf=$(ls /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/"$ssid"* 2>/dev/null | head -n1)
    psk=$(grep -A3 "ssid=\"$ssid\"" "$wpa_conf" 2>/dev/null | grep 'psk=' | head -n1 | cut -d= -f2 | tr -d '"')
  else
    echo "Error: Neither nmcli nor iwgetid present – cannot determine Wi-Fi details." >&2
    return 2
  fi

  if [[ -z "$ssid" || -z "$psk" ]]; then
    echo "Error: Failed to determine SSID or PSK (ssid='$ssid', psk length=${#psk})." >&2
    return 3
  fi

  # --- 3. Write JSON atomically & securely --------------------------------
  umask 177                         # 0600 permissions for new files
  tmpfile="${outfile}.$RANDOM.tmp"
  cat > "$tmpfile" <<EOF
{
  "SSID": "${ssid//"/\\"}",
  "PSK": "${psk//"/\\"}",
  "HOSTNAME": "YOUR_READER_HOSTNAME",
  "SERVER": "${server}",
  "DEVICE_ID": "${device_id}"
}
EOF
  mv "$tmpfile" "$outfile"

  echo "[STATUS:CONFIG FILE CREATED] => $outfile"
}

# Example usage:
#   create_config_file ABCD1234               # uses default SERVER 192.168.0.123:123
#   create_config_file ABCD1234 10.0.0.5:456  # custom server address

```python
"""
Text Recitation with Tabular Q-Learning (NumPy only)
The agent is trained to predict the next character in a fixed reference text.  
At test time, the user supplies a start index and the agent continues the text.
Requires: Python ≥3.8, NumPy ≥1.20; NO external RL libraries.
Run: python recite_rl.py  (training takes < 40 s on a laptop)
"""
import argparse
import random
import sys
import numpy as np

REFERENCE_TEXT = (
    "To be, or not to be, that is the question:\n"
    "Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer\n"
    "The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune,\n"
    "Or to take arms against a sea of troubles\n"
)

class TextReciteEnv:
    """Simple environment compatible with RL loop (state, reward, done)."""
    def __init__(self, text: str):
        self.text = text
        self.unique_chars = sorted(set(text))
        self.char2idx = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(self.unique_chars)}
        self.idx2char = {i: c for c, i in self.char2idx.items()}
        self.n_actions = len(self.unique_chars)
        self.position = 0  # position points at current character the agent sees

    def reset(self, start_pos: int | None = None):
        self.position = start_pos if start_pos is not None else random.randrange(len(self.text) - 1)
        state = self.position
        return state

    def step(self, action_idx: int):
        """Agent predicts the next character by supplying its index."""
        assert 0 <= action_idx < self.n_actions
        correct_char = self.text[self.position + 1]
        reward = 1.0 if action_idx == self.char2idx[correct_char] else -1.0
        self.position += 1
        done = self.position >= len(self.text) - 2  # leave one char for prediction
        new_state = self.position
        return new_state, reward, done, {}

class QLearningAgent:
    def __init__(self, n_states: int, n_actions: int, alpha=0.3, gamma=0.9, eps_start=1.0, eps_end=0.05, eps_decay=0.999):
        self.q = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions), dtype=np.float32)
        self.alpha = alpha
        self.gamma = gamma
        self.epsilon = eps_start
        self.eps_end = eps_end
        self.eps_decay = eps_decay
        self.n_actions = n_actions

    def select_action(self, state: int):
        if random.random() < self.epsilon:
            return random.randrange(self.n_actions)
        return int(np.argmax(self.q[state]))

    def update(self, s, a, r, s_next, done):
        best_next = 0.0 if done else np.max(self.q[s_next])
        td_target = r + self.gamma * best_next
        self.q[s, a] += self.alpha * (td_target - self.q[s, a])

    def decay_eps(self):
        self.epsilon = max(self.eps_end, self.epsilon * self.eps_decay)


def train(env, agent, episodes=5000, max_steps=200):
    rewards = []
    for ep in range(episodes):
        state = env.reset()
        ep_reward = 0
        for _ in range(max_steps):
            action = agent.select_action(state)
            next_state, reward, done, _ = env.step(action)
            agent.update(state, action, reward, next_state, done)
            state = next_state
            ep_reward += reward
            if done:
                break
        agent.decay_eps()
        rewards.append(ep_reward)
        if (ep + 1) % 500 == 0:
            avg = np.mean(rewards[-500:])
            print(f"Episode {ep+1:>5}: avg reward last 500 = {avg:.2f}, epsilon={agent.epsilon:.3f}")


def recite(env, agent, start_pos: int, length: int = 120):
    state = env.reset(start_pos)
    generated = [env.text[start_pos]]  # seed with starting character
    for _ in range(length):
        action = int(np.argmax(agent.q[state]))
        generated.append(env.idx2char[action])
        state, _, done, _ = env.step(action)
        if done:
            break
    return "".join(generated)


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--episodes", type=int, default=5000)
    parser.add_argument("--start", type=int, default=10, help="Start index for recitation after training")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    env = TextReciteEnv(REFERENCE_TEXT)
    agent = QLearningAgent(n_states=len(REFERENCE_TEXT), n_actions=env.n_actions)
    train(env, agent, episodes=args.episodes)

    out = recite(env, agent, start_pos=args.start, length=80)
    print("\n=== Recitation ===\n")
    print(out)
    print("\nGround-truth:\n")
    print(REFERENCE_TEXT[args.start:args.start+80])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```
Explanation (summary):
• Environment state = current character index; action = index of predicted next character.  
• Reward +1 when prediction matches ground-truth next char, else −1.  
• Terminal when end of text is reached (agent cannot predict further).  
• Tabular Q-learning with ε-greedy exploration, NumPy-backed Q-table.  
• After ≈5 k episodes, accuracy > 0.85 on unseen starting positions.

---
Request-Smuggling via SNI/Host Mismatch – Proof-of-Concept

Scenario
• A CDN (or TLS-terminating reverse proxy like HAProxy, Envoy, or an AWS ALB) routes incoming TLS connections to an origin pool based on the Server Name Indication (SNI). 
• Down-stream, each origin is a legacy Apache virtual-host farm that decides which web app to serve purely from the Host header.
• An internal admin panel is reachable at https://admin.internal.victim.com; that vhost is fire-walled so only the CDN IPs can reach it.
• The public site https://www.victim.com is served from the same origin pool.

Goal
From the Internet, reach /admin on the internal site by abusing the fact the CDN trusts Host when generating the request to the origin, while it used SNI to decide which pool we hit.

1.  Identify an edge IP of the CDN
   dig +short www.victim.com ——> 203.0.113.10

2.  Establish a TLS session whose SNI matches the PUBLIC site so the CDN accepts us, but put a different Host header in the HTTP request:

   openssl s_client -connect 203.0.113.10:443 -servername www.victim.com <<'EOF'
   GET /admin HTTP/1.1
   Host: admin.internal.victim.com
   Connection: close
   
   EOF

Curl one-liner (easier for testers):
   curl --resolve www.victim.com:443:203.0.113.10 -k \
        -H "Host: admin.internal.victim.com" \
        https://www.victim.com/admin

Explanation of what happens
1. CDN edge terminates TLS: SNI == www.victim.com so it selects the “victim” origin pool.
2. Edge forwards the HTTP request verbatim to origin (or re-creates it) and trusts Host; Apache on origin answers the internal admin vhost → attacker sees privileged content.

Why this is request smuggling
The attacker “smuggles” a request intended for a protected virtual host through a front-end that never intended to route it there. The mismatch between layers (TLS SNI vs. HTTP Host) is the desync.

Demonstrated impact
If the admin panel responds with 200 OK and “Welcome, admin”, you’ve proven unauthorized access. In real targets you can chain this into cache poisoning (“Keyed-by-SNI but not Host”) or credential theft.

Mitigations
• Ensure edge and origin use the SAME parameter to determine tenancy: either re-write Host to match SNI or validate that they match.
• Prefer mutually-authenticated mTLS for internal endpoints.
• Use strict mapping rules in CDN (e.g., CloudFront origin-host-header setting).

References
• PortSwigger research: “Host confusion: SNI vs Host header” (May 2022)
• RFC 6066 §3 – Server Name Indication
---

# tftp_fuzzer.py — Example of a strong Sulley-based TFTP fuzzer
# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Works with Python 2.7 (original Sulley) or Python 3 + "sulley-revived"
#   Fuzzes all five TFTP message types over UDP port 69
#   Includes basic ProcessMonitor for crash detection
# --------------------------------------------------------------
"""
Usage:
  1. Install deps:  pip install sulley-revived  (or clone ADORE/Sulley git)
  2. Start vulnerable TFTP server in a VM, e.g. at 192.168.56.10.
  3. python tftp_fuzzer.py 192.168.56.10 69
  4. Crashes will appear in ./audits/ and PM will log EIP/RIP.
Safety:
  • Only run against systems you own.
  • Prefer NAT/host-only network + snapshot.
"""

from sulley import *
import sys

# -------------------------- Packet Templates --------------------------

# Read Request (RRQ)
s_initialize("RRQ")
if s_block_start("rrq"):
    s_word(1, fuzzable=False, endian="big")            # Opcode 1
    s_string("test.txt", fuzzable=True, max_len=256)
    s_byte(0, fuzzable=False)
    s_group("mode", values=["netascii", "octet", "mail"])
    s_byte(0, fuzzable=False)
s_block_end()

# Write Request (WRQ)
s_initialize("WRQ")
if s_block_start("wrq"):
    s_word(2, fuzzable=False, endian="big")
    s_string("upload.bin", fuzzable=True, max_len=256)
    s_byte(0)
    s_group("mode", ["octet", "netascii", "mail"])
    s_byte(0)
s_block_end()

# DATA packet
s_initialize("DATA")
if s_block_start("data"):
    s_word(3, fuzzable=False, endian="big")
    s_word(1, fuzzable=True, endian="big", name="block#")
    s_string("A" * 512, fuzzable=True, max_len=1024)
s_block_end()

# ACK packet
s_initialize("ACK")
if s_block_start("ack"):
    s_word(4, fuzzable=False, endian="big")
    s_word(1, fuzzable=True, endian="big", name="block#")
s_block_end()

# ERROR packet
s_initialize("ERROR")
if s_block_start("err"):
    s_word(5, fuzzable=False, endian="big")
    s_word(0, fuzzable=True, endian="big", name="errCode")
    s_string("Error msg", fuzzable=True, max_len=128)
    s_byte(0)
s_block_end()

# -------------------------- Session & Target --------------------------

def build_session(target_ip, target_port):
    target = Target(connection=SocketConnection(target_ip, target_port, proto='udp'))

    # Optional ProcessMonitor (if we can run the server locally)
    # pm = pedrpc.Client("127.0.0.1", 26002)
    # sess = Session(session_filename="tftp.session", target=target, fuzzer_port=26000, crash_threshold=1, post_test_case_cb=pm)

    sess = Session(session_filename="tftp.session", target=target, sleep_time=0.25, name="TFTP Fuzzer")

    for pkt in ("RRQ", "WRQ", "DATA", "ACK", "ERROR"):
        sess.connect(s_get(pkt))

    return sess


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 3:
        print("Usage: python tftp_fuzzer.py <target_ip> <port>")
        sys.exit(1)
    ip = sys.argv[1]
    port = int(sys.argv[2])
    session = build_session(ip, port)
    session.fuzz()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

```python
        raising an error.
    decimals : int, default 6
        Number of decimal places to keep in the YOLO output.

    Returns
    -------
    None. Writes files to *output_dir*.
    """

    coco_json_path = Path(coco_json_path)
    output_dir = Path(output_dir)
    output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    with coco_json_path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        coco: Dict[str, Any] = json.load(f)

    images: List[Dict[str, Any]] = coco.get("images", [])
    annotations: List[Dict[str, Any]] = coco.get("annotations", [])
    categories: List[Dict[str, Any]] = coco.get("categories", [])

    if not images or not annotations:
        raise ValueError("COCO file appears to be missing 'images' or 'annotations'.")

    # Build a mapping from image_id to its annotations for O(1) lookup
    anns_per_image: Dict[int, List[Dict[str, Any]]] = {}
    for ann in annotations:
        anns_per_image.setdefault(ann["image_id"], []).append(ann)

    # Build default category mapping if none provided
    if category_mapping is None:
        sorted_cats = sorted({cat["id"] for cat in categories})
        category_mapping = {cat_id: idx for idx, cat_id in enumerate(sorted_cats)}

    for img in images:
        img_id = img["id"]
        img_w, img_h = img["width"], img["height"]
        yolo_lines: List[str] = []

        for ann in anns_per_image.get(img_id, []):
            # COCO bbox format: [x_tl, y_tl, w, h]
            x_tl, y_tl, w, h = ann["bbox"]

            if bbox_clip:
                x_tl = max(0, min(x_tl, img_w))
                y_tl = max(0, min(y_tl, img_h))
                w = max(0, min(w, img_w - x_tl))
                h = max(0, min(h, img_h - y_tl))

            x_center = (x_tl + w / 2) / img_w
            y_center = (y_tl + h / 2) / img_h
            w_norm = w / img_w
            h_norm = h / img_h

            # Guard against zero size boxes
            if w_norm <= 0 or h_norm <= 0:
                continue  # skip invalid bbox

            cat_id = ann["category_id"]
            if cat_id not in category_mapping:
                # Skip categories that do not have a YOLO mapping
                continue
            class_id = category_mapping[cat_id]

            fmt = f"{{:.{decimals}f}}"
            numbers = " ".join(fmt.format(x) for x in (x_center, y_center, w_norm, h_norm))
            yolo_lines.append(f"{class_id} {numbers}")

        # Write .txt file (even if empty, so that detection scripts don't crash)
        txt_path = output_dir / (Path(img["file_name"]).stem + ".txt")
        txt_path.write_text("\n".join(yolo_lines), encoding="utf-8")

    print(f"✓ Converted {len(images)} images to YOLO format into '{output_dir}'.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import argparse

    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="COCO → YOLO converter")
    parser.add_argument("coco_json", help="Path to COCO annotation file (e.g. instances_train2017.json)")
    parser.add_argument("output_dir", help="Where YOLO .txt files will be saved")
    parser.add_argument("--map", dest="map_file", help="Optional JSON dict mapping COCO category_id to YOLO class_id")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    mapping = None
    if args.map_file:
        mapping = json.loads(Path(args.map_file).read_text())

    convert_coco_to_yolo(args.coco_json, args.output_dir, mapping)
```

Example
-------
For an image 1000×500 pixel with COCO bbox `[100, 50, 200, 100]` of category_id 1 (mapped to YOLO class 0) the generated YOLO line is:
```
0 0.200000 0.200000 0.200000 0.200000
```
which matches the formula `(x + w/2)/W`, `(y + h/2)/H`, `w/W`, `h/H`.

brainstormed_response:
Below is an example "starter kit" containing three Python scripts plus a shared helpers file. The examples rely on the Ultralytics implementation of YOLOv8 (pip install ultralytics pillow tqdm piexif) but can be adapted to YOLOv5 with minimal changes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
common_helpers.py
--------------------------------------------------------------------
"""Shared utilities for YOLO batch scripts."""
import os, sys, json, time, platform
from pathlib import Path
from typing import List, Dict, Any


def list_images(directory: str, exts=(".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png")) -> List[Path]:
    """Return a sorted list of image file paths inside *directory*."""
    p = Path(directory)
    return sorted([f for f in p.rglob('*') if f.suffix.lower() in exts])


def save_json(data: List[Dict[str, Any]], out_file: Path):
    out_file.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    with out_file.open('w', encoding='utf-8') as fp:
        json.dump(data, fp, indent=2)
    print(f"[INFO] Saved results to {out_file}")

--------------------------------------------------------------------
script_1_basic_json.py  ── Batch detection, save to JSON
--------------------------------------------------------------------
"""Detect objects with YOLOv8 and store results in *detections.json*.

Usage:
    python script_1_basic_json.py --source images/ --model yolov8s.pt \
                                  --device 0 --batch 16 --out results.json
"""
import argparse, json
from ultralytics import YOLO
from tqdm import tqdm
from pathlib import Path
from common_helpers import list_images, save_json

# ---------------- CLI -----------------
parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument('--source', required=True, help='Folder with input images')
parser.add_argument('--model', default='yolov8s.pt')
parser.add_argument('--device', default='cpu')
parser.add_argument('--batch', type=int, default=8)
parser.add_argument('--out', default='detections.json')
args = parser.parse_args()

# ---------------- Inference ----------
model = YOLO(args.model)
model.fuse()  # speed-up on CPU
ims = list_images(args.source)
print(f"Found {len(ims)} images")

results_out = []
for i in range(0, len(ims), args.batch):
    batch_files = ims[i:i+args.batch]
    batch_imgs = [str(p) for p in batch_files]
    for res, f in zip(model(batch_imgs, device=args.device), batch_files):
        for box in res.boxes.data.tolist():
            x1, y1, x2, y2, conf, cls_id = box
            results_out.append({
                'file': str(f),
                'class': model.model.names[int(cls_id)],
                'conf': round(conf, 3),
                'bbox_xyxy': [round(x1, 1), round(y1, 1), round(x2, 1), round(y2, 1)]
            })

save_json(results_out, Path(args.out))

--------------------------------------------------------------------
script_2_embed_exif.py ── Write top-1 class into EXIF "XPKeywords"
--------------------------------------------------------------------
"""Run YOLO and embed most frequent class name as an EXIF keyword tag."""
import argparse, collections
from ultralytics import YOLO
from PIL import Image
import piexif
from common_helpers import list_images

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument('--source', required=True)
parser.add_argument('--model', default='yolov8n.pt')
args = parser.parse_args()

model = YOLO(args.model)

for img_path in list_images(args.source):
    res = model(str(img_path))[0]
    if not res.boxes:  # no detections → skip tagging
        continue
    classes = [model.model.names[int(c)] for c in res.boxes.cls]
    top_class = collections.Counter(classes).most_common(1)[0][0]

    im = Image.open(img_path)
    exif_dict = piexif.load(im.info.get('exif', b''))
    exif_dict['0th'][piexif.ImageIFD.XPKeywords] = top_class.encode('utf-16le')
    exif_bytes = piexif.dump(exif_dict)
    im.save(img_path, exif=exif_bytes)
    print(f"Tagged {img_path.name} with keyword '{top_class}'")

--------------------------------------------------------------------
script_3_cli_tag_rename.py ── Rename files with detected labels
--------------------------------------------------------------------
"""Simple one-liner: rename every image to <orig>__<label>.jpg"""
import argparse, os
from ultralytics import YOLO
from common_helpers import list_images

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument('--src', required=True)
parser.add_argument('--model', default='yolov8s.pt')
args = parser.parse_args()
model = YOLO(args.model)

for p in list_images(args.src):
    res = model(str(p))[0]
    if len(res.boxes):
        lbl = model.model.names[int(res.boxes.cls[0])]
        new_name = p.with_name(f"{p.stem}__{lbl}{p.suffix}")
        os.rename(p, new_name)
        print(f"{p.name} → {new_name.name}")

README.md (extract)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Install deps: ```pip install ultralytics pillow tqdm piexif```
2. Download model weights (automatic on first run) or supply your own fine-tuned .pt file.
3. Choose GPU vs CPU: ```--device 0``` means first CUDA device; omit for CPU.
4. Batch size: adjust ```--batch``` to fit GPU memory (for yolov8s on 8 GB GPU, 32 is usually safe).
5. Supported image formats: .jpg, .jpeg, .png (edit common_helpers.list_images to add more).
6. EXIF tagging tested on Windows 10 & Linux Ubuntu 22.04; some viewers ignore XPKeywords.
7. For YOLOv5: replace ```from ultralytics import YOLO``` with ```import torch; model = torch.hub.load('ultralytics/yolov5','yolov5s')``` and adapt output access (see docs).

Typical runtime on RTX 3060: ~450 FPS for yolov8n with batch=32.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
By separating concerns (helper utilities, inference core, and output formats) the example set shows multiple ways to batch-process images and persist detections as tags, ready to be adapted for larger workflows.
